entries.title: 6.5 — How AI Handles Voice
entries.summary: You've probably noticed: talking to Siri in 2020 felt like talking to a machine. Talking to ChatGPT's voice mode in 2025 feels like talking to a person — it laughs, it pauses, it picks up on your tone. Same concept (speak to AI, get spoken answer back), completely different experience. Why?…
entries.sourceText: You've probably noticed: talking to Siri in 2020 felt like talking to a machine. Talking to ChatGPT's voice mode in 2025 feels like talking to a person — it laughs, it pauses, it picks up on your tone. Same concept (speak to AI, get spoken answer back), completely different experience. Why? Because they use fundamentally different pipelines — and which pipeline you're using determines everything about how natural, responsive, and expressive the interaction feels. Pipeline 1: Transcribe → Think → Speak Back (the chain) 📼 Rewind it: This chain can feel like a late-'90s phone tree: one specialist takes the message, passes it on, and another delivers the reply. Each handoff can lose tone or detail before the next step begins. A native voice model shortens that chain; it does not become human or understand you the way a person does. This is how most voice assistants worked historically, and many still work this way: Your voice → [Speech-to-text model] → Text → [Language model] → Text response → [Text-to-speech model] → Audio you hear Three separate models in sequence, each doing one job: Step 1 — Speech-to-text (ASR): A model trained on thousands of hours of recorded speech paired with written transcripts. It hears your audio waveform and predicts which words you said. (Whisper by OpenAI is a well-known example — trained on 680,000 hours of multilingual audio.) Step 2 — Language model: Reads the text transcription. Generates a text response. Has no idea you spoke it — just sees text. All your tone, hesitation, emphasis, accent — lost in transcription. Step 3 — Text-to-speech (TTS): Takes the text response and generates audio that sounds like a human voice. Trained on recordings of voice actors reading scripts. The output has appropriate pacing and emphasis, but it was generated from text — it has no awareness of how YOU spoke. The problem with this chain: Each handoff loses information. Your sarcastic tone becomes flat text. The model's witty response becomes generic speech synthesis. There's latency at every junction (transcribe... think... synthesize...). And the three models can't coordinate — the speech model doesn't know what the language model is about to say, so it can't prepare. This is why Siri and Alexa often feel robotic and slow — it's three separate systems passing notes. Pipeline 2: Native Audio (voice-to-voice, end-to-end) This is what GPT-4o introduced in 2024 — one model that processes audio tokens directly: Your voice → [Audio tokens directly into the model] → [Model generates audio tokens directly] → Audio you hear One model, end-to-end. The audio itself is tokenised — sound waves chopped into tiny time slices (about 100ms each), encoded as tokens — and fed directly into the same model that handles text. The model was trained on audio alongside text, so it processes both natively. What this means mechanically: The model "hears" your tone, pace, emphasis, hesitation, laughter It generates audio with appropriate intonation, emotion, pacing — not just reading text aloud It can be interrupted mid-sentence and respond naturally (real-time processing) Latency is much lower (one model, not three in a chain) It can express surprise, amusement, urgency in its voice because it's generating audio directly, not converting text to speech This is why GPT-4o's voice mode felt like talking to a person — you could interrupt, it could laugh, it matched your energy. The model isn't reading a script. It's generating voice the same way it generates text: token by token, each one informed by everything that came before. 🔍 Concept in Practice: Why talking to Siri feels different from talking to ChatGPT voice mode Siri is Pipeline 1 — three models passing notes. There's a noticeable pause after you speak (transcription), another pause while it thinks (generation), and the voice that comes back sounds "read aloud" rather than "spoken naturally." ChatGPT voice mode (GPT-4o) is Pipeline 2 — native audio processing. The response starts before you've even fully stopped talking, the tone matches the conversation, and it can handle overlapping speech, laughter, and emphasis. It's not smarter — it's architecturally different. Pipeline 3: Voice Cloning and Text-to-Speech Generation Separate from conversation — this is "generate audio that sounds like a specific person's voice." A model is trained on samples of a target voice (sometimes just a few seconds, sometimes hours of recordings) and learns to generate new speech in that voice from any text input. This is how: AI audiobook narration works (train on a voice actor's existing recordings, generate new books) Voice translation works ("speak this text in French, but keep it sounding like the original English speaker") Deepfake audio is created (a concerning application — realistic fake audio of real people)

entries.title: 6.6 — Video: Diffusion in Motion
entries.summary: Video generation (Sora by OpenAI, Kling, Runway) works the same way as image diffusion — but adds a dimension. Instead of denoising a 2D image (width × height), the model denoises a 3D block (width × height × time). The noise is added and removed across frames as well as pixels.…
entries.sourceText: Video generation (Sora by OpenAI, Kling, Runway) works the same way as image diffusion — but adds a dimension. Instead of denoising a 2D image (width × height), the model denoises a 3D block (width × height × time). The noise is added and removed across frames as well as pixels. Image diffusion Video diffusion Pure noise (one frame of static) Pure noise (many frames of static) Remove noise step by step → single clear image Remove noise step by step → sequence of clear frames Cross-attention guided by text → "a library" Cross-attention guided by text → "a library, camera panning left" Spatial coherence (pixels relate to neighbours) Spatial AND temporal coherence (pixels relate to neighbours AND to the same region in adjacent frames) The extra challenge: temporal consistency. Each frame needs to be internally coherent (look like a real image) AND consistent with the frames before and after it (objects don't teleport, lighting doesn't randomly change, motion is smooth). This is why: Video generation is much more expensive than image generation (3D denoising, many more tokens) Generated videos often have subtle flickering or objects that "morph" slightly between frames — temporal consistency is harder than spatial consistency Generated videos are currently short (a few seconds to a minute) — longer videos compound the consistency problem 🔍 Concept in Practice: Why AI-generated videos still feel "off" Even when individual frames look photorealistic, the motion between frames can feel uncanny. A person's arm might drift subtly. A background object might shift position. Physics might not quite work (liquid pouring wrong, fabric moving unnaturally). This is because the model is making statistically plausible frames — each one looks right in isolation — but maintaining perfect physical consistency across time is a much harder constraint than making one good image.

entries.title: 6.7 — Why "Native Multimodal" Feels Different
entries.summary: Some AI systems handle multiple types by chaining separate specialist models: An image tool uses one model for vision, a different one for language A voice assistant uses three separate models (transcribe, think, speak) An image editor uses a language model to interpret your request, then passes instructions to a diffusion model Other systems — the frontier multimodal models of 2026 — handle everything in one system: Approach How it wor…
entries.sourceText: Some AI systems handle multiple types by chaining separate specialist models: An image tool uses one model for vision, a different one for language A voice assistant uses three separate models (transcribe, think, speak) An image editor uses a language model to interpret your request, then passes instructions to a diffusion model Other systems — the frontier multimodal models of 2026 — handle everything in one system: Approach How it works Feels like Chained specialists Separate models for each type, passing results between them Three people passing notes in a relay — slower, information lost at each handoff Native multimodal One model trained on text + images + audio together One person who reads, sees, and hears simultaneously — faster, nothing lost in translation Native multimodal models can do things chained systems can't: Look at an image and talk about it with awareness of both visual and textual context simultaneously Generate an image mid-conversation that references things discussed in text earlier Process your voice, understand your words, AND notice your emotional tone — all in one pass Seamlessly switch between input/output types without losing context This is the direction all frontier models are heading. GPT-4o, Claude, and Gemini are all natively multimodal in 2026 — they were trained on mixed streams of text, images, and audio together, not retrofitted with separate modules.

entries.sourceText: You now understand how AI processes and generates different types of content — text, images, audio, video. You know what happens mechanically when you upload a photo, generate an image, talk to an AI, or ask it to edit something. But all of this — the vision encoder, the diffusion process, the voice pipeline, the language model — is doing work in the background every time you press send. That work takes time, costs money, and uses computational resources. Some requests are fast and cheap. Others are slow and expensive. Chapter 7 takes you inside what happens the moment you actually press send — the process called inference — and explains why some responses stream in instantly while others take 30 seconds, why companies charge by the token, and why inference (not training) is where most of the money is being spent.

entries.title: 📖 Key Terms — Quick Reference
entries.summary: Vision encoder Chops an image into patches and converts each patch into numbers a language model can read. How AI "sees." Diffusion model Generates images by starting from random noise and gradually removing it, guided by your text prompt. Forward diffusion The training process: take a real image and progressively add noise until it's pure static. The model learns to reverse this.…
entries.sourceText: Vision encoder Chops an image into patches and converts each patch into numbers a language model can read. How AI "sees." Diffusion model Generates images by starting from random noise and gradually removing it, guided by your text prompt. Forward diffusion The training process: take a real image and progressively add noise until it's pure static. The model learns to reverse this. Reverse diffusion (denoising) The generation process: start from noise and sculpt it step by step into a coherent image. More steps = more detail. Cross-attention The mechanism connecting your text prompt to the image generation process. At each denoising step, the model checks which words are relevant to which region of the image. How words steer pixels. Inpainting Editing only a masked region of an image while leaving the rest untouched. The model generates new content for the masked area that blends with the surroundings. img2img Using an existing image as the starting point instead of pure noise. Lower strength = closer to original; higher strength = more creative freedom. ASR (automatic speech recognition) Converting spoken audio into text. The first step in Pipeline 1 (traditional voice systems). TTS (text-to-speech) Converting text into spoken audio. The last step in Pipeline 1. Native audio tokens Processing voice directly as audio tokens without converting to text first. How Pipeline 2 works (GPT-4o, modern voice modes). Enables interruption, tone matching, and natural conversation. Multimodal A model trained on multiple types of input/output (text, images, audio, video) together, not retrofitted with separate modules. The direction all frontier models are heading. Pipeline 1 vs Pipeline 2 Pipeline 1: three separate models (speech-to-text → language model → text-to-speech). Pipeline 2: one model processing audio natively. Pipeline 2 is why modern AI voice feels like talking to a person rather than dictating to a machine. Check your understanding Question: A model describes an image. Did it literally see it as a person does? Answer: No. It converted the image into numerical representations and learned relationships between those representations and language.

entries.title: 7.1 — Training Was School. This Is the Job.
entries.summary: In Chapter 5, you learned how a model gets built: billions of examples, the guess-check-adjust loop, months of compute, millions of dollars. All of that work produces a single thing — a file of frozen weights. Now the model is done. It's deployed. It's running on servers somewhere.…
entries.sourceText: In Chapter 5, you learned how a model gets built: billions of examples, the guess-check-adjust loop, months of compute, millions of dollars. All of that work produces a single thing — a file of frozen weights. Now the model is done. It's deployed. It's running on servers somewhere. And you open a chat window and type: "What's the best way to get coffee stains out of a white shirt?" What happens next is inference — the model applying its learned patterns to your input and generating a response. No learning happens. No weights change. The model isn't getting smarter from your question. It's running your tokens through its frozen numbers and producing output. The relationship between training and inference: Training Inference What it does Builds the model (adjusts weights) Uses the model (applies frozen weights) When it happens Once (or occasionally, for updates) Every single time someone uses the system How long Weeks to months Seconds Cost per occurrence $50M–$1B+ for frontier models Fractions of a cent per request But at scale... One-time capital expense Ongoing operational cost — scales with every user Inference is where most of the money goes — not training. Training is eye-wateringly expensive per run, but it happens once. Inference happens billions of times per day, every day, for as long as the product exists. Gartner reported in August 2026 that for the first time, global spending on inference infrastructure ($23.3 billion) has overtaken training ($19 billion). The cost of using AI now exceeds the cost of building it. By the end of this chapter, you will be able to: Explain the difference between training (building the model) and inference (using it) Describe what actually happens — step by step — when you press "send" on a message Understand why the same prompt can give different answers each time Explain why some responses are fast and others are slow Understand why inference (not training) is where most of the money goes at scale

entries.title: 7.2 — What Happens When You Press "Send"
entries.summary: Let's trace your message through the system, step by step. You type: "What's the best way to get coffee stains out of a white shirt?" Step 1: Your message gets tokenised The text is split into tokens (Chapter 4). Your question becomes a sequence of maybe 15–20 tokens.…
entries.sourceText: Let's trace your message through the system, step by step. You type: "What's the best way to get coffee stains out of a white shirt?" Step 1: Your message gets tokenised The text is split into tokens (Chapter 4). Your question becomes a sequence of maybe 15–20 tokens. These get combined with other things already in the context window: The system instructions (hidden instructions telling the model how to behave) The conversation history (everything you and the model have said so far) Any documents or files you've attached The current date/time (injected by the application layer) Any tool results (if the system searched the web before answering) All of this — your new message plus everything else — forms the complete input. This could be hundreds or thousands of tokens. Step 2: Prefill (the model reads your input) The model processes the entire input in a single pass. All those tokens flow through the network's layers simultaneously — this is where the transformer's parallel processing (Chapter 5) pays off. The model builds an internal representation of what you're asking: the context, the meaning, the relationships between words. During this step, the model also creates a KV cache — a set of "scratch notes" about each token. These notes will be reused during generation so the model doesn't have to re-read the entire input for each new word it produces. ⏸️ "What's a KV cache, actually?" Remember attention (Chapter 5) — where each token calculates how relevant every other token is? That calculation produces two things for each token: a Key (which says "this is what I contain") and a Value (which says "this is what I contribute when attended to"). During prefill, the model computes these Keys and Values for every input token. Then it saves them. During generation, when the model is producing the 50th output token, it needs to attend to all previous tokens (your input + the 49 tokens it's already generated). Without the cache, it would have to recompute the Keys and Values for all previous tokens from scratch — every single step. With the cache, it just looks up the saved notes. Massively faster. It's like taking notes during a lecture so you don't have to re-listen to the whole recording every time you want to check a fact. Prefill is fast relative to what comes next, because it processes all input tokens in parallel. Step 3: Decode (the model generates a response, one token at a time) Now the model starts producing output. The key: it generates one token at a time. Each new token depends on everything before it — the input plus all the tokens it has already generated. The process at each step: The model calculates a probability for every token in its vocabulary (~100,000 options). It applies temperature and sampling settings (more on this in a moment) to narrow the choices. It picks one token. That token gets appended to the sequence. Back to step 1 for the next token. This continues until the model produces a stop signal (a special token that means "I'm done") or hits a length limit. This is why you see responses appear piece by piece in a chat interface. The model is not writing the whole response and then revealing it. It generates one token at a time, and the interface updates as tokens arrive. A token may be a whole word, part of one, punctuation or another reusable piece, so the visible updates do not map neatly to one word each. 🔍 Concept in Practice: Why responses stream piece by piece When an AI response appears gradually, you are watching the decode phase reach the interface. The model selects one token, appends it, then repeats. The product may display one token immediately or batch several into a smoother update, so a visible word is not proof of one token. A pause can reflect next-token computation, tool use, network delay or interface batching; the animation is not a window into human-style thought.

entries.title: 7.3 — Why the Same Prompt Gives Different Answers
entries.summary: 📼 Rewind it: Turning temperature down is a Miranda Priestly edit pass: fewer next-word options are allowed onto the runway, so the result is usually more consistent. That does not make it more intelligent, more factual, or automatically correct. Ask the same question twice and you'll often get different responses. entries.sourceText: 📼 Rewind it: Turning temperature down is a Miranda Priestly edit pass: fewer next-word options are allowed onto the runway, so the result is usually more consistent. That does not make it more intelligent, more factual, or automatically correct. Ask the same question twice and you'll often get different responses. Not just different words — sometimes genuinely different content, structure, or reasoning paths. Why? Because generation isn't deterministic. At each step, the model is looking at ~100,000 possible next tokens, each with a different likelihood. It doesn't always pick the most likely one. Instead, it draws from a weighted lottery — tokens with higher likelihood are more likely to be picked, but it's not guaranteed. Like drawing a name from a hat where some names are on more slips than others. Temperature is the main dial that controls this: Temperature = 0 (or very low): The model almost always picks the highest-probability token. Responses are consistent, predictable, and repetitive. Ask the same thing twice, get nearly the same answer. Temperature = 1 : The model samples normally from its learned distribution. Good balance of variety and coherence. Temperature > 1 : The model flattens the distribution — less-likely tokens get a bigger chance. Responses become more creative, surprising, and potentially incoherent. Think of it like this: at low temperature, the model only picks from the obvious choices. At high temperature, it's willing to take riskier, less conventional options. Top-k and Top-p are additional filters: Top-k : Only consider the k most likely next tokens (e.g., top 40). Everything else gets zero probability, regardless of how reasonable it might be. Top-p (also called nucleus sampling): Only consider tokens whose cumulative probability adds up to p (e.g., 0.9). This adapts — sometimes that's 5 tokens, sometimes 500, depending on how confident the model is. In practice, you rarely control these yourself — the application (ChatGPT, Claude, etc.) sets them based on the task. But now you know why two people asking the same question get different answers, and why AI-generated text doesn't feel robotic — it's because there's controlled randomness baked into every single token choice. ⏸️ Wait — so it's just randomly picking words? Not randomly — probabilistically. The probabilities come from the patterns learned during training. The model knows that after "The capital of France is" the token "Paris" has very high probability. It's not random that it picks "Paris" — the randomness only matters when multiple tokens are similarly plausible. "The best way to remove coffee stains is" could reasonably continue with "vinegar" or "baking soda" or "cold water" — and which one it picks on any given run is where the sampling randomness enters.

entries.title: 7.4 — Why Some Responses Are Slow (and Others Aren't)
entries.summary: You've probably noticed: sometimes an AI responds almost instantly, other times there's a noticeable delay. What determines the speed? What makes inference faster: Shorter input — less to process in the prefill phase Shorter output — fewer tokens to generate one-by-one in the decode phase Smaller model — fewer parameters to run the maths through Better hardware — faster chips process tokens more quickly Cached context — if the system in…
entries.sourceText: You've probably noticed: sometimes an AI responds almost instantly, other times there's a noticeable delay. What determines the speed? What makes inference faster: Shorter input — less to process in the prefill phase Shorter output — fewer tokens to generate one-by-one in the decode phase Smaller model — fewer parameters to run the maths through Better hardware — faster chips process tokens more quickly Cached context — if the system instructions haven't changed since last time, the KV cache can be reused What makes inference slower: Long conversation history — everything in the context window gets processed every time Long output — a 2,000-word essay takes longer to generate than a yes/no answer because it's 2,000 sequential token predictions Large model — more parameters = more computation per token High traffic — when millions of people are using the system simultaneously, requests queue up Latency is what you feel as a user — the time between pressing send and seeing the first token appear. For current frontier models, this is typically 0.5–2 seconds for the first token, then 30–100 tokens per second streaming after that. Throughput is what the company cares about — how many simultaneous requests the system can serve. This is where hardware, batching, and engineering determine whether the system can handle 10 users or 10 million.

entries.title: 7.5 — Batching: Serving Millions at Once
entries.summary: When only one person is using the system, inference is straightforward — run their tokens through the model, generate a response. But ChatGPT alone handles hundreds of millions of conversations per week. Thousands of requests arrive every second. How do you serve all of them without needing a separate GPU for each person? Batching.…
entries.sourceText: When only one person is using the system, inference is straightforward — run their tokens through the model, generate a response. But ChatGPT alone handles hundreds of millions of conversations per week. Thousands of requests arrive every second. How do you serve all of them without needing a separate GPU for each person? Batching. Instead of processing one request at a time (like a restaurant that only seats one table at once), the system groups multiple requests together and processes them simultaneously on the same GPU (like a restaurant that seats forty tables and has a kitchen running orders in parallel). What makes this work mechanically: remember that inference has two phases (section 7.2) — prefill (reading all the input) and decode (generating output token by token). At any given moment, different users are at different stages. User A is in prefill (their input is being read). User B is on their 15th output token. User C is on their 200th. The GPU can work on all three simultaneously because they're all just matrix multiplications on different sets of numbers — and GPUs (Chapter 16) do thousands of multiplications in parallel by nature. Modern inference engines (like vLLM, TensorRT-LLM) are specifically designed to maximise this: they continuously add new requests to the batch as old ones finish, keeping the GPU at near-100% utilisation. A single GPU that takes 2 seconds to serve one user might serve 50 users in those same 2 seconds through batching — not by going faster, but by doing all their work simultaneously. The trade-off: batching increases throughput (more users served) but can slightly increase latency (each individual request might wait a fraction longer). Systems balance this constantly based on traffic.

entries.title: 7.6 — The Economics: Why Inference Is Where the Money Goes
entries.summary: The cost split is counterintuitive: Training: Eye-wateringly expensive once. A frontier model costs $200M–$1B+ to train. But you do it once (or occasionally for model updates). It's a capital investment. Inference: Cheap per request. A single conversation costs fractions of a cent. But multiply by millions of users, millions of requests per day, every day, for years — and inference becomes the dominant cost.…
entries.sourceText: The cost split is counterintuitive: Training: Eye-wateringly expensive once. A frontier model costs $200M–$1B+ to train. But you do it once (or occasionally for model updates). It's a capital investment. Inference: Cheap per request. A single conversation costs fractions of a cent. But multiply by millions of users, millions of requests per day, every day, for years — and inference becomes the dominant cost. By 2026, companies running AI at scale spend 70–90% of their AI compute budget on inference, not training. The training gets the headlines. The inference gets the bills. Why output tokens cost more than input tokens (something you noticed in Chapter 4's pricing tables): Input tokens (prefill): Processed in parallel. The model reads your entire prompt in one pass. Efficient. Output tokens (decode): Generated sequentially, one at a time, each depending on the last. The model can't parallelise this — it must wait for each token before predicting the next. More compute per token. That's why every API charges 3–10x more for output tokens than input tokens. It's not a pricing trick — it reflects the actual compute cost difference between reading (parallel) and writing (sequential). 🔍 Concept in Practice: Why AI subscription services limit "heavy" usage If you've hit usage limits on ChatGPT, Claude, or other AI services — being told you've sent too many messages or need to wait — now you know why. Each response you generate costs real compute (output tokens generated sequentially on expensive hardware). A subscription at $20/month is subsidising inference costs that could be $0.05–$1.00+ per long conversation. Heavy users sending hundreds of long messages per day can cost the company far more than the subscription covers. Usage limits are inference economics in action.

entries.summary: Let's put it all together. entries.sourceText: Let's put it all together. When you press send: Your message enters the system Tokenisation — your text is chopped into tokens Context assembly — your tokens are combined with system instructions, conversation history, tool results, and metadata (like the current date) Prefill — the model processes the full context in one parallel pass, building an internal representation Decode — the model generates output tokens one at a time, each sampled from a probability distribution shaped by temperature and top-p settings Streaming — generated tokens are delivered toward the interface as they become available; the product may display them individually or in small batches, so the response appears piece by piece rather than in a guaranteed one-word-per-token rhythm Stop — the model produces a stop token or hits its output limit. Response complete. The entire process takes 1–30 seconds depending on response length. No weights changed. No learning happened. The model is exactly the same after answering your question as before. It just ran your input through its frozen patterns and produced the most probable continuation.

Next, we'll look at how the raw trained model gets refined into something actually helpful — that's fine-tuning and RLHF.

entries.sourceText: Watch the streaming. Next time you use an AI chatbot, watch the response appear in pieces. That is the interface receiving live generated output, sometimes one token at a time and sometimes in small batches. The useful clue is that the answer is still being produced—not that each visible word equals one token. Now try this: ask the same question twice. Notice the responses are different — different wording, maybe different structure or examples. That's temperature and sampling at work. The model isn't broken — it's drawing from a probability distribution, and different draws produce different (but usually valid) outputs. A harder experiment: Ask a factual question with one correct answer ("What's the capital of Japan?") — you'll get the same answer every time because the probability distribution heavily favours "Tokyo." Now ask an open-ended creative question ("Write me a short poem about coffee") — you'll get a different poem every time because many tokens are similarly plausible at each step.

It might ramble, or refuse to answer, or respond in a format you didn't want.…

entries.summary: Inference Using the trained model. Applying frozen weights to new input. No learning happens. "Training is school. Inference is the job." Prefill Phase 1: the model reads your entire input in one parallel pass, building an internal representation and KV cache. entries.sourceText: Inference Using the trained model. Applying frozen weights to new input. No learning happens. "Training is school. Inference is the job." Prefill Phase 1: the model reads your entire input in one parallel pass, building an internal representation and KV cache. Decode Phase 2: the model generates output tokens one at a time, sequentially. This is why output costs more than input. Temperature Controls randomness. Low = predictable (always picks the most likely token). High = creative/surprising (willing to pick less likely tokens). Doesn't change what the model knows — just how it samples from what it knows. Top-k Only consider the k most probable next tokens. Everything else gets zero chance. Top-p (nucleus sampling) Only consider tokens whose cumulative probability reaches p. Adapts to confidence: when the model is sure, fewer options; when uncertain, more. Latency Time from pressing send to seeing the first word. Determined by input size, model size, hardware speed, and traffic. Throughput How many requests the system handles simultaneously. Determined by hardware, batching, and system design. Batching Grouping multiple users' requests to process simultaneously on the same hardware. Increases throughput. KV cache "Scratch notes" the model keeps about each token during prefill, so it doesn't have to re-read the entire input when generating each new output token. Check your understanding Question: Why might the same prompt produce two plausible but different answers? Answer: Inference samples from learned probabilities; decoding settings and context can change which continuation is selected.

entries.title: 8.1 — The Model Remembers Nothing
entries.summary: Let's start with something that surprises most people: the model has no memory. When you have a conversation with ChatGPT or Claude, it feels like the system remembers what you said earlier. You mention your name at the start, and it uses your name later. You describe a problem in message 1, and it references it in message 10. It seems like it's remembering. It isn't.…
entries.sourceText: Let's start with something that surprises most people: the model has no memory. When you have a conversation with ChatGPT or Claude, it feels like the system remembers what you said earlier. You mention your name at the start, and it uses your name later. You describe a problem in message 1, and it references it in message 10. It seems like it's remembering. It isn't. What's actually happening: Every time you send a new message, the product assembles a new context for that request. It may include your new message, system instructions and some earlier conversation, but it can drop, summarise or omit older material. The model works from whatever the product supplies on that turn; it is not privately recalling the whole transcript from its own memory. This is why, in Chapter 5, we said the model is stateless — it's a recipe that runs fresh every time. You pour your ingredients in (the tokens), the recipe runs (the weights do their work), output comes out. Then the kitchen is wiped clean. Nothing lingers between requests. The "memory" you experience is the application layer (ChatGPT's interface, Claude's interface) saving your conversation transcript and feeding the whole thing back in as input each time you send a new message. 🔍 Concept in Practice: Why starting a new conversation "resets" the AI When you open a new chat, the AI doesn't know who you are, what you were working on, or what you discussed yesterday. That's because the previous conversation's transcript isn't in the new context window. The model hasn't forgotten — it never knew in the first place. New chat, new context: "We were on a break!" Each conversation is a completely isolated context window. What was in the old window doesn't carry over unless something explicitly moves it. By the end of this chapter, you will be able to: Explain why AI has no memory by default — and what "memory" actually means when companies claim to offer it Describe the difference between knowledge (frozen in weights) and context (provided live each time) Explain what embeddings are and how they let machines measure "similarity" Understand how RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) gives a model access to information it wasn't trained on Describe why "the model knows things" is misleading — and what's actually happening

Memory (in AI) Not actual memory — information stored externally and re-injected into the context window each time. The model itself remembers nothing. Embedding A list of numbers that represents the meaning of a piece of text — arranged so that similar meanings sit near each other Vector A list of numbers. An embedding is a specific type of vector that encodes meaning. Vector database A specialised database that stores embeddings and lets you search by similarity — "find me things similar to this" RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) A system that retrieves relevant documents, injects them into the context window, and lets the model generate a response grounded in that information Semantic search Searching by meaning rather than by exact keywords — "find documents about the same concept , even if they use different words"

entries.title: 8.2 — The Two Sources of "Knowledge"
entries.summary: Based on everything you've learned so far, there are only two ways the model "knows" something when it responds to you: Source 1: Training weights (frozen, general, potentially stale) Everything the model absorbed during training (Chapters 3-5) is encoded in its weights. This includes patterns of language, general facts about the world, reasoning patterns, style — everything that was in the training data.…
entries.sourceText: Based on everything you've learned so far, there are only two ways the model "knows" something when it responds to you: Source 1: Training weights (frozen, general, potentially stale) Everything the model absorbed during training (Chapters 3-5) is encoded in its weights. This includes patterns of language, general facts about the world, reasoning patterns, style — everything that was in the training data. This knowledge is frozen at the training cutoff date and never updates. Source 2: Context window (live, specific, provided right now) Everything placed into the context window for this specific request — your message, conversation history, system instructions, documents you uploaded, search results, the current date. This is live information, specific to this moment, and disappears the moment the response is complete. The model can't tell the difference. When it generates a response, it draws on both sources simultaneously. It doesn't flag "this fact comes from my training" versus "this fact comes from the document you just uploaded." It processes everything in the context window as one combined input. This distinction — training knowledge vs contextual information — is fundamental to understanding both the capabilities and limitations of these systems.

entries.title: 8.3 — What "Memory" Actually Means (When Companies Say It)
entries.summary: 📼 Rewind it: Calling every saved preference "memory" is how you end up with a Burn Book full of assumptions. Ask what was actually stored, where it lives, and whether the product will retrieve it next time. The model itself has not quietly become a person who remembers you. In 2024–2026, many AI products launched "memory" features — ChatGPT's Memory, Claude's memory, and others. What are these actually doing?…
entries.sourceText: 📼 Rewind it: Calling every saved preference "memory" is how you end up with a Burn Book full of assumptions. Ask what was actually stored, where it lives, and whether the product will retrieve it next time. The model itself has not quietly become a person who remembers you. In 2024–2026, many AI products launched "memory" features — ChatGPT's Memory, Claude's memory, and others. What are these actually doing? They're not giving the model actual memory. They're doing this: Extracting facts from your conversations ("User's name is Ali." "User prefers concise answers." "User is working on a textbook project.") Storing those facts externally — in a database, outside the model. Injecting relevant facts back into the context window each time you start a new conversation. The model still has no memory. But the application layer remembers things about you and feeds them back in each time, making it appear as if the model remembers. It's a clever design — but mechanically, it's just context window management. The three tiers of AI "memory" (as of 2026): Tier What it is Where it lives In-context The current conversation. Everything the model can see right now. Inside the context window (disappears when the conversation ends) Semantic memory Stored facts about you, your preferences, your projects. External database. Injected into context window when relevant. Episodic memory Records of past interactions — what you discussed, when, what was decided. External database. Retrieved and injected when relevant. All three tiers ultimately work the same way: information gets placed into the context window so the model can see it. The model itself is always stateless. The sophistication is in what gets stored and what gets retrieved — not in the model gaining actual memory. ⏸️ Wait — so it could "forget" things it supposedly memorised? Yes. If the memory system fails to retrieve a fact, or if the context window is too full to include it, the model won't have access to it — even if it's stored in the database. "Memory" in AI is retrieval, not storage inside the model. Anything that isn't in the current context window might as well not exist.

entries.title: 8.4 — Embeddings: Turning Meaning Into Numbers
entries.summary: Here's a problem the system needs to solve: you've uploaded 500 documents and asked a question. The system needs to figure out which of those documents are relevant to your question — without reading all 500 every time (that would blow the context window and cost a fortune). How would you solve this? Think of a library.…
entries.sourceText: Here's a problem the system needs to solve: you've uploaded 500 documents and asked a question. The system needs to figure out which of those documents are relevant to your question — without reading all 500 every time (that would blow the context window and cost a fortune). How would you solve this? Think of a library. If books were shelved in the order they were purchased, finding anything relevant would mean scanning every single shelf. But libraries don't work that way. They put books about similar topics near each other — dog training next to puppy behaviour, French cooking next to Italian cooking. If you know where one relevant book is, everything nearby is probably relevant too. Embeddings do this for text — but instead of a physical shelf with spatial proximity, they use a space made of numbers. Every piece of text gets placed somewhere in this numerical space, arranged so that texts with similar meanings sit near each other. The technical name for "a piece of text's location in this space" is an embedding — a list of numbers (typically 1,000–3,000 of them) that represents where this text sits in meaning-space. What that looks like concretely: Example: The sentence "How do I remove coffee stains?" might become the vector [0.23, -0.87, 0.41, 0.12, ...] The sentence "What's the best way to clean coffee off fabric?" — even though it uses completely different words — would get a very similar vector [0.24, -0.85, 0.39, 0.14, ...] The sentence "What's the capital of France?" would get a very different vector [-0.56, 0.33, -0.71, 0.88, ...] The embedding model has learned (through its own training) that the first two sentences mean the same thing — so it places them near each other in number-space. The third sentence means something entirely different, so it lands far away. What's remarkable — and somewhat unexplained — is how well this works. The model wasn't taught a theory of meaning. It was trained on enormous amounts of text and somehow developed numerical representations where proximity genuinely corresponds to semantic similarity. It works across languages, across domains, even across concepts that were never explicitly paired in training. Why this produces such useful similarity measurements is not fully understood — but the practical result is that you can search millions of documents by meaning, not just by keywords, and get relevantly matched results. How "near" and "far" are measured: The system calculates how close together two sets of numbers are. Close numbers = similar meaning. Far-apart numbers = different meaning. (The specific technique is called cosine similarity — you don't need to know the maths, just that it's a reliable way to measure "how similar are these two things?") This is how machines do "similarity" — not by understanding meaning the way you do, but by placing meanings in a numerical space where closeness = relatedness.

entries.title: 8.5 — Vector Databases: The Similarity Search Engine
entries.summary: Once you can turn text into embeddings, you need somewhere to store them and search through them. That's a vector database. A vector database stores thousands or millions of text chunks (documents, paragraphs, notes, previous conversations), each one converted to an embedding. When you ask a question, your question also gets embedded, and the database finds the stored chunks whose embeddings are closest to your question's embedding.…
entries.sourceText: Once you can turn text into embeddings, you need somewhere to store them and search through them. That's a vector database. A vector database stores thousands or millions of text chunks (documents, paragraphs, notes, previous conversations), each one converted to an embedding. When you ask a question, your question also gets embedded, and the database finds the stored chunks whose embeddings are closest to your question's embedding. This is semantic search — searching by meaning rather than keywords. You don't need to use the exact same words as the stored document. You just need to ask about the same concept , and the embedding similarity will find the relevant information. Example flow: You have 500 company documents, each split into paragraphs. Each paragraph gets embedded (turned into a vector of ~1,500 numbers) and stored in a vector database. A user asks: "What's our refund policy for damaged items?" That question gets embedded. The vector database finds the 3–5 stored paragraphs whose embeddings are most similar. Those paragraphs get injected into the context window. The model generates a response grounded in those specific documents. The model didn't "know" your refund policy from training. It was given the relevant information in its context window, retrieved via embedding similarity.

entries.title: 8.6 — RAG: Retrieval-Augmented Generation
entries.summary: 📼 Rewind it: Elle Woods does not win because she sounds confident; she wins because she brings the relevant evidence into the room. Retrieval gives a model material to work from at answer time. You still check whether it fetched the right, current material. The flow described above has a name: RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation). It's one of the most important architectural patterns in production AI (2024–2026).…
entries.sourceText: 📼 Rewind it: Elle Woods does not win because she sounds confident; she wins because she brings the relevant evidence into the room. Retrieval gives a model material to work from at answer time. You still check whether it fetched the right, current material. The flow described above has a name: RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation). It's one of the most important architectural patterns in production AI (2024–2026). The problem RAG solves: The model's training knowledge is frozen (stale, general, potentially wrong) The model can't access your company's documents, your emails, your databases You need the model to answer questions grounded in specific, current, private information The RAG pipeline: User asks a question ↓ Question gets embedded (turned into a vector) ↓ Vector database searched for similar chunks ↓ Top matching chunks retrieved ↓ Chunks injected into the context window alongside the question ↓ Model generates a response using both its training knowledge AND the retrieved context ↓ User gets an answer grounded in actual documents Let's watch it work — a real example, step by step: You're using your company's AI assistant. You ask: "What's our parental leave policy?" Your question gets embedded. A small, fast embedding model converts "What's our parental leave policy?" into a vector — say, [0.31, -0.72, 0.18, ...] (1,536 numbers that represent the meaning of your question). Vector database searched. The system compares your question's vector against thousands of pre-embedded chunks from your company's HR documents. It calculates similarity scores. The chunk about parental leave scores 0.94 (very similar meaning). The chunk about vacation policy scores 0.71. The chunk about the office dress code scores 0.12 (irrelevant — distant in meaning-space). Top chunks retrieved. The system grabs the top 3–5 most similar chunks. In this case: the parental leave policy paragraph, the related benefits overview, and the FAQ about leave extensions. Chunks injected into context. These chunks get placed into the context window alongside your question. The model now sees: `` [System instructions] + [Retrieved: "Parental leave: 20 weeks paid for birthing parents, 6 weeks for non-birthing parents, extendable to 12 with manager approval..."] + [Your question: "What's our parental leave policy?"] `` Model generates. The model reads everything in the context window — your question AND the retrieved policy document — and generates a response grounded in that specific text: "Your parental leave policy provides 20 weeks paid leave for birthing parents and 6 weeks for non-birthing parents, with the option to extend to 12 weeks with manager approval." Response delivered. You get an answer grounded in the policy text the system retrieved — even though the model was never trained on your HR documents. You still need to check that it retrieved the right, current passages and represented them correctly. Total time: ~1.5 seconds. What made it possible: embedding + similarity search + context injection. The model didn't "know" your policy. It read it, right then, because the RAG pipeline put it in front of the model at the right moment. Why this matters: RAG is how AI products answer questions about your data — your company's knowledge base, your notes, your files. The model wasn't trained on your documents. But it doesn't need to be — the documents get retrieved and placed into context in real time. The model reads them on the fly and generates an answer. This is also how AI systems stay current despite their knowledge cutoff. A RAG system can retrieve today's news article and inject it into context — the model reads it and can answer questions about it, even though it was published after training ended. 💡 Training vs RAG — two ways to give a model information Training: Bake patterns into the weights. Expensive, slow and frozen once done. Good for general knowledge and capabilities. RAG: Retrieve selected information at answer time and inject it into context. It can use newer, specific or private material without retraining — but only if the source collection is current and the system retrieves the right passages. Most production AI systems use both: a pre-trained model plus retrieval for information needed now. Neither route guarantees a correct answer.

entries.title: 8.7 — Why "The Model Knows Things" Is Misleading
entries.summary: You now have the full picture to understand why this phrase is misleading: When someone says "GPT knows about World War II" or "Claude knows Python" — what's actually happening is: during training, the model absorbed statistical patterns from text about WWII or Python code. Those patterns are encoded in its weights. When you ask a question, those patterns produce tokens that look like knowledge. But: It has no concept of truth.…
entries.sourceText: You now have the full picture to understand why this phrase is misleading: When someone says "GPT knows about World War II" or "Claude knows Python" — what's actually happening is: during training, the model absorbed statistical patterns from text about WWII or Python code. Those patterns are encoded in its weights. When you ask a question, those patterns produce tokens that look like knowledge. But: It has no concept of truth. It generates the most probable next tokens based on patterns — which are usually correct for well-documented topics, but can be wrong. It can't verify what it's saying. It has no mechanism for checking its output against reality. It doesn't "know" in the way you know. You can introspect ("am I sure about this?"). The model can't — it just generates with whatever confidence the patterns produce. When the model is wrong — when it "halluccinates" a fact, invents a citation, or confidently states something false — it's not lying. It's producing the most probable token sequence given its patterns, and those patterns happen to generate something that isn't true. There's no internal flag that says "I'm making this up." 🔍 Concept in Practice: Why AI invents fake citations Ask an AI to "give me three academic papers about X with full citations" and it will often produce author names, paper titles, journal names, and years — that don't exist. The generated text looks exactly like a real citation (correct format, plausible author names, real journal names) because the patterns of what citations look like are strong in training data. But the specific combination of author + title + year was never verified against reality. The model generated what a citation should look like — not what actually exists. This is pattern-completion without a truth-check.

entries.title: 8.9 — Try This
entries.summary: Test the "no memory" principle. Open a new conversation with any AI chatbot. Ask it: "What's my name?" It won't know — because nothing in the context window tells it. Now tell it your name, have a short conversation, then start a new conversation and ask again. Gone. The first conversation's context isn't in the new window. Test semantic search thinking.…
entries.sourceText: Test the "no memory" principle. Open a new conversation with any AI chatbot. Ask it: "What's my name?" It won't know — because nothing in the context window tells it. Now tell it your name, have a short conversation, then start a new conversation and ask again. Gone. The first conversation's context isn't in the new window. Test semantic search thinking. Think of two sentences that mean the same thing but use completely different words: "I need to cancel my subscription" "How do I stop my monthly payments?" A keyword search for "cancel subscription" wouldn't find the second one (no matching words). A semantic search using embeddings would — because the meaning is the same. That's the power embeddings give to retrieval systems. A harder question: If the model generates a wrong answer, is the problem more likely to be (a) bad patterns in the weights, or (b) missing or irrelevant context in the window? The answer is usually (b) — and that's why RAG and better context management are where most improvement comes from in practice, not retraining the model.

entries.title: 8.10 — What's Next
entries.summary: You now know that the model is stateless and that all "knowledge" comes from either frozen weights or live context. You know how embeddings and vector databases let systems find relevant information. You know how RAG injects that information into the model's view. But a raw pre-trained model — even with great context — still isn't great to use. It might be rude, unhelpful, or produce harmful content.…
entries.sourceText: You now know that the model is stateless and that all "knowledge" comes from either frozen weights or live context. You know how embeddings and vector databases let systems find relevant information. You know how RAG injects that information into the model's view. But a raw pre-trained model — even with great context — still isn't great to use. It might be rude, unhelpful, or produce harmful content. It doesn't know how to follow instructions reliably. It doesn't know what "be helpful" means. Chapter 9 takes us to fine-tuning and RLHF: the process of taking a model that can generate text and teaching it to be helpful, harmless, and honest — to follow instructions, to refuse harmful requests, and to admit when it doesn't know something.

entries.title: 9.1 — The Spectrum: Cheapest to Most Expensive
entries.summary: Say you're using an AI chatbot at work and it keeps getting your company's refund policy wrong. entries.sourceText: Say you're using an AI chatbot at work and it keeps getting your company's refund policy wrong. It confidently tells customers they have 60 days to return items when the actual policy is 30 days. It's costing you complaints. You have options. You could rephrase your instructions to be clearer — that's free and takes thirty seconds. You could feed it the actual policy document so it has the right information — that takes a few days to set up. You could retrain the model on thousands of examples of correct customer service responses — that costs real money and takes weeks. Or you could build an entirely new model from scratch — but nobody does that unless they have hundreds of millions of dollars and a very good reason. Those options aren't random. They sit on a spectrum — from cheapest and fastest to most expensive and powerful — and knowing where to start (and when to move down) is one of the most practical things you can learn about using AI in the real world. Here's the spectrum, from lightest to heaviest: Level What it is Cost Time Who does it 1. Prompting Phrase your question well Free Seconds Anyone 2. Few-shot prompting Include examples in your prompt Free Minutes Anyone 3. System instructions Set behaviour rules the model follows every time Free Minutes Anyone with access 4. RAG Retrieve relevant documents into context Low–medium Days to weeks to build Engineers 5. Fine-tuning Train further on specific data (adjusts weights) $100–$100K+ Days to weeks ML engineers 6. RLHF / DPO Shape behaviour through human preference ratings $50K–$1M+ Weeks to months Specialised teams 7. Full pre-training Train an entire model from scratch $50M–$1B+ Months Only a handful of companies The key insight from industry practice (2026): start at the top and only move down when you've genuinely exhausted the lighter options. Most problems can be solved with prompting + RAG. Fine-tuning is for behaviour changes that can't be encoded in a prompt. Full pre-training is almost never the right answer unless you're building a foundation model company. The 2026 rule of thumb: prompt first, retrieve for knowledge, fine-tune for behaviour. By the end of this chapter, you will be able to: Describe the full spectrum of ways to customise an AI system — from free and fast to expensive and powerful Explain when you'd use prompting vs RAG vs fine-tuning vs full training Understand how RLHF and DPO shape a model's behaviour after pre-training Explain what distillation, quantisation, and mixture of experts do and why they matter Use a decision framework: "Given what I need, which approach makes sense?"

entries.title: 9.2 — Prompting and Few-Shot (Levels 1–2)
entries.summary: Try this: ask an AI system to summarise a long document. You'll get a summary. Now ask the same system the same question, but this time add: "Summarise this in exactly 3 bullet points, each under 15 words, focusing only on financial implications." You'll get a dramatically different — and likely more useful — response. Nothing changed about the model. You changed how you asked.…
entries.sourceText: Try this: ask an AI system to summarise a long document. You'll get a summary. Now ask the same system the same question, but this time add: "Summarise this in exactly 3 bullet points, each under 15 words, focusing only on financial implications." You'll get a dramatically different — and likely more useful — response. Nothing changed about the model. You changed how you asked. That's prompting — and the gap between a lazy prompt and a precise one is often the gap between a useless answer and an excellent one. Zero-shot: You just ask directly. "Summarise this article." No examples, no special formatting. Works for straightforward tasks where the model's default behaviour is close enough to what you want. Few-shot: You include examples of what you want before asking. "Here are 3 customer emails and how I categorised them. Now categorise this 4th one." The model sees the pattern in your examples and applies it to the new case — without any retraining. This was the breakthrough that GPT-3 demonstrated in 2020: you could "program" the model just by writing examples in plain English. No code, no training, no waiting. The examples go into the context window, the model reads them, and it follows the pattern. It's shockingly effective. Why this works (mechanically): The model is a pattern-completion machine (Chapter 5). Its entire training was: given a sequence of tokens, predict what comes next. Show it a pattern of input→output pairs, and it continues that pattern — because that's literally the only thing it knows how to do. Three examples of "email → category" followed by a fourth email? The most probable next tokens are the correct category. The model isn't "reasoning about categorisation." It's completing a pattern it was shown. When it's not enough: When you need a model version to make a particular format or tone more likely across many interactions without sending the same examples every time. Prompts and examples are supplied in the context for each request. If those instructions are long and repeated at scale, fine-tuning may be worth testing — but changing the weights does not guarantee that the model will follow the pattern every time.

entries.title: 9.3 — RAG (Level 4) — Giving It Knowledge Without Retraining
entries.summary: Back to that refund policy problem from the start of this chapter. The chatbot says 60 days when it should say 30. Why is it wrong? Because the correct policy isn't in its training data — the model was trained on the internet, not on your internal HR documents. It's guessing based on whatever refund policies it saw during training.…
entries.sourceText: Back to that refund policy problem from the start of this chapter. The chatbot says 60 days when it should say 30. Why is it wrong? Because the correct policy isn't in its training data — the model was trained on the internet, not on your internal HR documents. It's guessing based on whatever refund policies it saw during training. RAG (Chapter 8) solves this directly: instead of hoping the model "knows" your policy, you retrieve the actual document and inject it into the context window. The model reads it right there, in real time, and answers based on what it just read — not what it vaguely remembers from training. You've already seen the full mechanism in Chapter 8. In the context of the customisation spectrum, here's the key distinction: What RAG changes: What information the model can use for this request. It can give the model access to selected specific, newer or private information that was not stored in its trained weights. The answer still depends on the source collection, retrieval and generation all working well. What RAG doesn't change: The trained weights of the model version. Retrieved material can influence the answer, wording and format for this request, but RAG alone does not create a newly trained model version. The practical test: If the request needs information the model was not trained on, investigate retrieval. If the same format or tone keeps failing after good instructions and examples, test whether fine-tuning improves that recurring tendency. Many products use both, and neither should be chosen without evaluation.

entries.title: 9.4 — Fine-Tuning (Level 5) — Changing How It Behaves
entries.summary: Here's a situation where prompting and RAG both fail: you're building a medical chatbot that needs to respond in a specific clinical format — SOAP notes (Subjective, Objective, Assessment, Plan). You write it into the system prompt: "Always respond in SOAP format." It works... 80% of the time. The other 20%, the model slips back into conversational style. You add more emphatic instructions. It helps a little. You add examples.…
entries.sourceText: Here's a situation where prompting and RAG both fail: you're building a medical chatbot that needs to respond in a specific clinical format — SOAP notes (Subjective, Objective, Assessment, Plan). You write it into the system prompt: "Always respond in SOAP format." It works... 80% of the time. The other 20%, the model slips back into conversational style. You add more emphatic instructions. It helps a little. You add examples. Better, but still not 100%. The problem is that you're fighting against the model's trained behaviour — its weights (Chapter 5) encode patterns from billions of examples of normal conversation, and your prompt is trying to override all of that with a few sentences of instruction. Sometimes the override holds. Sometimes the deeper pattern wins. Fine-tuning changes the model version itself. Instead of supplying the same instruction only in the current request, you train on examples of the behaviour you want and adjust the model's weights before later use. That can make SOAP-format responses more likely without repeating the full example set each time. Thousands of examples later: "What, like it's hard?" It does not make the format automatic: the fine-tuned model still needs testing on real and unfamiliar cases. A rough analogy: prompting is like bringing a phrase card for this conversation; fine-tuning is more like practising the language before later conversations. Practice can make a response pattern more likely, but the person can still slip — and a model can too. When you'd use it: You need a consistent output format across thousands of responses (e.g. always respond in JSON, always use a specific medical terminology style) and prompting isn't reliable enough You need a model version to favour a domain-specific tone or vocabulary across many requests, and prompting alone is not reliable enough Repeated instructions are making every request long, and testing shows a fine-tuned model can meet the task with shorter inputs; measure the actual speed, quality and cost rather than assuming a saving You have proprietary examples of exactly how you want the model to respond — hundreds or thousands of input→output pairs that demonstrate the behaviour What it costs (2026): Anywhere from a few hundred dollars (fine-tuning a small model on a small dataset) to $100K+ (fine-tuning a large model on a substantial dataset with many examples). The cost depends on model size × dataset size × number of training epochs. Most companies start with 500–2,000 examples and a few hundred dollars — enough to see if the approach will work before investing more. What it doesn't do: It doesn't teach the model new facts reliably. This is counter-intuitive — you'd think "train it on our company's data" would teach it about your company. But fine-tuning is better at shaping behaviour (style, format, tone, decision patterns) than at injecting knowledge (new facts about the world). Why? Because reliable factual recall requires the information to be reinforced across many training examples in many contexts — a few hundred examples about your company isn't enough to compete with billions of tokens of general training. For knowledge, use RAG. For behaviour, use fine-tuning. For both, combine them. 💡 The Rule: Prompt for instructions, RAG for knowledge, fine-tune for behaviour Need the model to follow specific instructions? → Better prompting. Need it to know about your documents/data? → RAG. Need it to consistently behave differently (format, style, tone, domain patterns)? → Fine-tuning. In practice, production systems often combine all three: a fine-tuned model + RAG for knowledge + good system prompts for per-request instructions.

entries.title: 9.5 — RLHF: How Human Feedback Shapes Behaviour
entries.summary: Here's something Chapter 3 promised we'd return to: RLHF — Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback. After pre-training, a model can generate text — but it doesn't know what "helpful" means. It might produce toxic content (because that was in the training data). It might ignore your instructions (because instruction-following wasn't its training task). It might be verbose, evasive, or inconsistent.…
entries.sourceText: Here's something Chapter 3 promised we'd return to: RLHF — Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback. After pre-training, a model can generate text — but it doesn't know what "helpful" means. It might produce toxic content (because that was in the training data). It might ignore your instructions (because instruction-following wasn't its training task). It might be verbose, evasive, or inconsistent. RLHF is the process that shapes the model into something actually pleasant to use. Here's how it works: Step 1: Collect human preferences. Show human evaluators two possible responses to the same prompt. Ask: "Which one is better?" Repeat this thousands of times across many different prompts and response pairs. Step 2: Train a reward model. Use those human preferences to train a separate model — a "reward model" — that can predict what humans would prefer. This model learns patterns like: helpful > evasive, concise > rambling, accurate > wrong, safe > harmful. Step 3: Adjust the main model to match what humans preferred. The system adjusts the main model's weights (the recipe amounts from Chapter 5) so it produces responses that score highly according to the reward model. The model learns: "responses that look like this get rewarded; responses that look like that get penalised." It's like training a new employee by showing them examples of work that got praised vs work that got corrected — over time, they produce more of the praised kind. The result: A model version whose responses have been shaped toward preferences such as helpfulness, instruction-following and safer refusal behaviour. Those are tendencies, not guarantees, and providers can use different combinations of preference-training methods. What's honestly strange about this: RLHF works better than anyone fully understands. Models trained with preference data sometimes exhibit behaviours that weren't explicitly in the preference examples — they generalise from "humans preferred A over B in these 50,000 cases" to broader behavioural patterns that nobody directly taught. Why this generalisation works as well as it does, and whether it will keep working as models get more capable, is an open question. Researchers use it because it produces good results — not because they can fully explain why the results are as good as they are.

entries.title: 9.6 — DPO and Constitutional AI: Simpler Alternatives
entries.summary: RLHF works, but it's complex — you need to train a separate reward model, then run reinforcement learning. Researchers have found simpler approaches: DPO (Direct Preference Optimisation): A more direct preference-training method. Instead of first training a separate reward model and then using reinforcement learning, DPO adjusts the model from pairs such as "humans preferred Response A over Response B." It pursues a similar broad aim wi…
entries.sourceText: RLHF works, but it's complex — you need to train a separate reward model, then run reinforcement learning. Researchers have found simpler approaches: DPO (Direct Preference Optimisation): A more direct preference-training method. Instead of first training a separate reward model and then using reinforcement learning, DPO adjusts the model from pairs such as "humans preferred Response A over Response B." It pursues a similar broad aim with a different training procedure; it does not promise an identical model or identical results. Constitutional AI (Anthropic's approach): Instead of using human raters for every preference judgement, you give the model a written "constitution" — a set of principles like "be helpful," "don't produce harmful content," "acknowledge uncertainty." Then you have the model judge its own outputs against those principles and learn from its self-evaluations. The constitution draws from sources like the UN Universal Declaration of Human Rights, Apple's terms of service, AI ethics research, and Anthropic's own guidelines. The model learns to critique and revise its own responses — a form of self-alignment. This approach is called RLAIF (Reinforcement Learning from AI Feedback) — the AI is providing its own feedback, guided by the constitution, rather than relying on human raters for every judgement. ⏸️ Wait — the AI judges itself? Isn't that circular? Partially. The model that does the judging uses the constitution as a guide — it's not just making things up. And the constitution was written by humans based on human values. So human values still enter the system — just through written principles rather than thousands of individual rating tasks. It's not purely circular, but it does require carefully written principles.

entries.title: 9.7 — Making Models Smaller and Faster
entries.summary: Not every improvement is about making models bigger. Several techniques make models smaller, cheaper, and faster to run: Distillation What it does: Takes a large, expensive model (the "teacher") and trains a smaller model (the "student") to mimic it. How it actually works: Run the teacher model on thousands of examples.…
entries.sourceText: Not every improvement is about making models bigger. Several techniques make models smaller, cheaper, and faster to run: Distillation What it does: Takes a large, expensive model (the "teacher") and trains a smaller model (the "student") to mimic it. How it actually works: Run the teacher model on thousands of examples. For each one, record not just the final answer but the full probability distribution — which tokens the teacher considered likely and how likely each one was. Train the student model to match those distributions — not just "get the right answer" but "rank the options the same way the teacher did." Why the full distribution matters: if the teacher sees "The capital of France is ___" and assigns 92% to "Paris," 3% to "the," 2% to "a" — that ranking contains more information than just "the answer is Paris." It tells the student how confident to be and what the near-misses were. Training on these "soft labels" transfers the teacher's uncertainty and nuance, not just its conclusions. Why it matters: A 3-billion-parameter model distilled from a much larger one can often match the larger model's quality on specific tasks — while being 10× cheaper and faster to run. This is how "phone-sized" AI models get made: distilled from the big ones. Quantisation What it does: Reduces the precision of the numbers in a model. Instead of storing each weight as a 16-bit number (high precision, takes more memory), you store it as a 4-bit or 8-bit number (less precision, takes less memory). What that means mechanically: A 16-bit number can represent 65,536 different values. A 4-bit number can only represent 16. Quantisation rounds every weight in the model to its nearest value in that smaller set — like rounding every price in a catalogue to the nearest dollar instead of tracking pennies. You lose some exactness, but you can fit 4× as many numbers in the same memory space. A model with 70 billion parameters stored in 16-bit takes ~140 GB of memory. Quantised to 4-bit, the same model fits in ~35 GB — suddenly within reach of a high-end consumer GPU instead of requiring a data centre rack. Why it matters: A quantised model uses 2–4× less memory and runs faster — often with minimal quality loss. This is what lets large models run on consumer hardware (a laptop GPU, a phone chip) rather than requiring expensive data centre equipment. The trade-off: Slight quality degradation. For most tasks, barely noticeable. For tasks requiring high precision (complex maths, very nuanced language), the rounding errors compound across billions of calculations and the quality difference shows. Mixture of Experts (MoE) The concept below is what matters — the mechanical details are optional depth. What it does: Instead of running every token through all parameters, MoE divides the model into "experts" — specialised sub-networks. For each token, a router decides which experts to activate (typically 2 out of 8, or similar). The rest stay dormant. How it actually works — step by step: Imagine a hospital. You walk in with a problem. You don't see every specialist in the building — you see a triage nurse (the router ) who looks at your symptoms and sends you to the right 1–2 departments. The orthopaedic surgeon and the dermatologist don't waste time on your sore throat. They exist, they're available if needed, but for your visit they stay idle. That's MoE. Here's the mechanism: A token arrives at a layer in the network. (Say the token is "photosynthesis.") The router — a tiny neural network — looks at that token and produces a score for each expert: "Expert 3 scores 0.8, Expert 7 scores 0.6, the rest score below 0.1." The system activates the top-k experts (usually top-2). Only Experts 3 and 7 process this token. Each active expert runs its own set of weights on the token and produces an output. The outputs are weighted and combined (Expert 3 contributed 57%, Expert 7 contributed 43% — proportional to their router scores). That blended result moves to the next layer. The other 6 experts never fired. The maths that matters: If a model has 8 experts per layer and activates 2, only 25% of the parameters do work on any given token. The model can have 1.8 trillion total parameters but run at the speed and cost of a ~220-billion-parameter dense model — because that's roughly how many parameters actually fire per token. Why it matters: You get the capacity of a huge model (trillions of total parameters) with the cost of a much smaller one (because only a fraction activates per token). GPT-4 (2023) reportedly used this architecture — according to widely-cited leaks (never officially confirmed by OpenAI), it had ~1.8 trillion total parameters across 16 experts, activating 2 per token (~220 billion active per token, or about 12.5% of total capacity). Most frontier models in 2026 use some form of MoE. The trade-off: MoE models use more total memory (all experts must be loaded even though most are idle per token). They're also harder to train — you need "load balancing" to prevent all tokens from routing to the same favourite expert while others atrophy from disuse. It's the architectural equivalent of making sure every department in the hospital still gets patients, not just the popular one. As of 2026: MoE is the dominant architecture for frontier language models. It's how the industry builds larger, more capable systems while keeping inference cost manageable. 🔍 Concept in Practice: Why some AI models "fit on your phone" When you see a model described as "runs locally on your device," it has typically been distilled (trained to mimic a bigger model) AND quantised (compressed to use less memory). A model that originally required hundreds of gigabytes of server memory can be compressed to 2–4 GB while retaining much of its capability for everyday tasks. That's why Apple Intelligence, Google's on-device features, and local AI apps work without an internet connection — they're running small, compressed versions of models that were originally enormous.

entries.title: 9.8 — Decision Framework: When to Use What
