entries.sourceText: A chatbot answers questions. You ask, it responds. One exchange. Done. An agent does work. It takes a goal, breaks it into steps, uses tools, evaluates its own progress, and keeps going until the job is done — or until it gets stuck and asks for help. The three things that make something an agent rather than a chatbot: Tools. The system can do things beyond generating text — search the web, read files, send messages, execute code, interact with other software. A loop. Instead of one-shot (question → answer), the system runs in a cycle: think about what to do → do it → observe the result → decide what to do next → repeat. It can take multiple actions in sequence without waiting for you to tell it each step. State and memory. The system maintains awareness of what it's already done, what it's tried, what worked, and what didn't — within a task and (sometimes) across tasks. A chatbot generates text. An agent generates text and takes actions and evaluates its own work and iterates until a goal is reached. By the end of this chapter, you will be able to: Explain what makes an agent different from a chatbot (tools + memory + a planning loop) Describe the agent loop: perceive → reason → act → observe → repeat Understand how "tool calling" works — how a model triggers real actions Explain what MCP (Model Context Protocol) is and why it standardises how agents connect to tools Describe the difference between single agents and multi-agent systems Understand where agents are now (2026) — what they can reliably do, and where they still struggle

entries.title: 14.2 — The Agent Loop

entries.sourceText: Every agent, regardless of how it's built, follows the same fundamental loop. Why a loop? Because the model can only do one thing per turn: generate text. It can't simultaneously search the web AND check a calendar AND compose an email. It does one thing, sees what came back, then decides what to do next. It's not iterating because it's uncertain (like a person) — it's iterating because that's mechanically how text generation works: one output at a time, each informed by what came before. The loop isn't a design choice someone made — it's a structural consequence of how these systems generate. You can't produce a ten-step plan in one shot when steps 3–10 depend on what step 1 returns from the real world. Here's the structure: Open the text version of this diagram ┌──────────────────────────────┐ │ │ ↓ │ [PERCEIVE] │ What do I know right now? │ What's in my context? │ ↓ │ [REASON / PLAN] │ What should I do next? │ Do I need a tool? Which one? │ ↓ │ [ACT] │ Call a tool, generate output, │ take an action │ ↓ │ [OBSERVE] │ What happened? What came back? │ Did it work? │ ↓ │ [DECIDE] │ Am I done? Or do I need │ another loop? │ │ │ └── (if not done) ────────────┘ A concrete example: "Book me the cheapest flight from Vancouver to Toronto next Friday." Perceive: I have the user's request. I need dates, route, and price comparison. Reason/Plan: I should search for flights, compare options, and present the cheapest. I'll use the flight search tool. Act: Call the flight search tool with parameters: YVR → YYZ, next Friday. Observe: Results come back — 6 flights, ranging from $289 to $712. Decide: I have the results. The cheapest is $289 on WestJet at 6:15am. But should I just tell the user, or book it? I'll present options and ask. That's one loop — but a complex task might involve 5, 10, or 50 loops before it's complete.

entries.title: 14.3 — Tool Calling: How a Model "Does Things"
entries.summary: The model itself can't search the web, send emails, or book flights. It can only generate text. So how does it "use tools"? Through tool calling — a specific format of text generation that the system interprets as an instruction to execute an action.…
entries.sourceText: The model itself can't search the web, send emails, or book flights. It can only generate text. So how does it "use tools"? Through tool calling — a specific format of text generation that the system interprets as an instruction to execute an action. How it works: The system prompt tells the model: "You have access to these tools: web_search(query), send_email(to, subject, body), calendar_create(title, date, time)." When the model decides it needs to use a tool, it generates structured text: {"tool": "web_search", "query": "cheapest flight YVR to YYZ August 22"} The harness (Chapter 10) intercepts this structured output, recognises it as a tool call, and executes the actual search. The results come back and get injected into the context window. The model sees the results and generates its next response (or makes another tool call). The key insight: The model doesn't execute anything. It generates text in a specific format. The system around the model (the harness) reads that text, executes the real action, and feeds the results back. The model's "power" to act comes entirely from the system built around it. A real example, step by step: You ask: "What's the weather like in Vancouver right now?" Step Who What happens 1 You Type your question 2 Model Reads the question + its system prompt (which says: "You have a weather_lookup tool"). Decides it needs current data it doesn't have in its weights. 3 Model generates Instead of answering directly, it outputs: {"tool": "weather_lookup", "location": "Vancouver, BC"} 4 Harness Sees the structured tool-call output. Pauses the model's generation. Makes an actual API call to a weather service. 5 Weather API Returns: {"temp": "18°C", "conditions": "partly cloudy", "humidity": "72%"} 6 Harness Injects this result back into the context window: "Tool result: temperature 18°C, partly cloudy, 72% humidity" 7 Model Sees the tool result in context. Resumes generating tokens. Produces: "It's 18°C (64°F) and partly cloudy in Vancouver right now, with 72% humidity." 8 You See the final response From your perspective, you asked a question and got an answer. Behind the scenes, the model generated text → the system intercepted it → an external action ran → results came back → the model finished its response. This all happens in 2-4 seconds. What makes agents different from a single tool call: an agent can do this multiple times in a row without your involvement. It might: Call tool A, read the results Decide it needs more information, call tool B Read those results, realise there's a conflict Call tool C to resolve the conflict Finally produce its answer to you Each cycle is the same pattern: model generates a tool call → harness executes → results injected → model continues. The loop is what makes it an agent. ⏸️ Wait — it just writes text and the system does the real thing? Yes. The model has no direct connection to the internet, your email, or any external system. It generates structured text (essentially instructions), and the harness follows those instructions. This is important: the model doesn't "decide" to send an email in any mechanical sense different from generating any other text. It produces tokens that, in context, are interpreted by the harness as an action request. The decision to actually execute is made by the harness layer, which is where guardrails, sandboxing, and human-in-the-loop checks live.

entries.title: 14.4 — MCP: The Standard for Connecting Tools
entries.summary: Before 2024, every integration between a model and a tool was custom-built. Want your agent to use Google Calendar? Write a custom integration. Want it to use Slack? Write another custom integration. Every tool, every model, every combination — bespoke code. MCP (Model Context Protocol) changed this.…
entries.sourceText: Before 2024, every integration between a model and a tool was custom-built. Want your agent to use Google Calendar? Write a custom integration. Want it to use Slack? Write another custom integration. Every tool, every model, every combination — bespoke code. MCP (Model Context Protocol) changed this. Introduced by Anthropic in November 2024 and donated to an industry-wide standards body in 2025, MCP is an open standard that defines a universal way for agents to discover and use tools. It's now the dominant way AI tools connect to each other — adopted across the industry within months. The analogy that's actually accurate: MCP is to AI tools what USB-C is to devices. Before USB-C, every device had its own proprietary charger. MCP gives every tool a standard "port" that any agent can plug into. How it works: Tools run on separate MCP servers (lightweight programs that expose capabilities) The agent connects to these servers at runtime The server tells the agent: "This is what I can do" (a list of available tools with descriptions) The agent can then call any of those tools using the standard protocol Results come back in a standard format By mid-2026: MCP SDK downloads passed 97 million monthly. It's become the default way agents connect to external systems.

entries.title: 14.5 — Planning and Decomposition
entries.summary: Simple tasks ("search for X") need one tool call. But real tasks ("plan a team offsite") require breaking the goal into sub-tasks: Check team members' availability Research venue options in the area Compare costs Draft an itinerary Send a proposal to the team This is planning — the ability to decompose a complex goal into an ordered sequence of steps, execute them one at a time, and adjust the plan based on what each step reveals.…
entries.sourceText: Simple tasks ("search for X") need one tool call. But real tasks ("plan a team offsite") require breaking the goal into sub-tasks: Check team members' availability Research venue options in the area Compare costs Draft an itinerary Send a proposal to the team This is planning — the ability to decompose a complex goal into an ordered sequence of steps, execute them one at a time, and adjust the plan based on what each step reveals. How agents plan (2026): Explicit decomposition: The model writes out a plan (numbered steps) before executing. It can then work through the steps and revise the plan as new information arrives. Implicit reasoning: For simpler tasks, the model just decides the next action at each loop without writing a full plan — reasoning step-by-step within the loop. Hierarchical planning: For very complex tasks, a "planner" agent creates the high-level plan and delegates sub-tasks to specialised "worker" agents. Where agents still struggle (2026): Very long plans (20+ steps) — errors compound, plans drift Tasks requiring precise sequencing where one mistake invalidates everything Knowing when to give up vs when to try a different approach Recovering from unexpected tool failures mid-task Why this is hard (the honest mechanical reason): The model doing the "reasoning" in the agent loop is a next-token predictor. It wasn't trained to plan — it was trained to produce plausible-sounding text. When it generates a plan, it's producing tokens that look like a plan (because it saw many plans in training data), not executing a planning algorithm. The difference matters: a real planner can verify that step 3 logically follows from step 2. A language model generating "step 3" is just producing the most probable continuation of the text that includes steps 1 and 2. It often works — because plans in training data were usually coherent. But it breaks on novel problems, unusual sequences, and edge cases where the "most probable next step" isn't the correct one. This is the deepest open question in agentic AI (2026): can next-token prediction learn to plan, or does reliable planning require a fundamentally different mechanism? Nobody knows. Some researchers argue that scale will solve it (bigger models plan better). Others argue that planning is algorithmically different from text generation and needs dedicated architectural components. Both camps have evidence. The field is building agents anyway — using scaffolding (retries, verification steps, human checkpoints) to compensate for the planning limitation.

entries.title: 14.6 — Multi-Agent Systems
entries.summary: Sometimes one agent isn't enough. Complex tasks benefit from multiple specialised agents working together: A researcher agent gathers information A writer agent produces content based on the research A reviewer agent checks the writer's work for accuracy A coordinator agent manages the workflow and routes tasks This is a multi-agent system — and it's how many of the most capable AI products work internally (2026).…
entries.sourceText: Sometimes one agent isn't enough. Complex tasks benefit from multiple specialised agents working together: A researcher agent gathers information A writer agent produces content based on the research A reviewer agent checks the writer's work for accuracy A coordinator agent manages the workflow and routes tasks This is a multi-agent system — and it's how many of the most capable AI products work internally (2026). When you ask a complex question that requires research, reasoning, and composition — the system might internally route your request through several specialised agents. A2A (Agent-to-Agent protocol): Just as MCP standardises how agents talk to tools, A2A (announced by Google in 2025) standardises how agents talk to each other — discovery, handoffs, status updates, and shared context between agents made by different companies. 🔍 Concept in Practice: Why complex AI tasks sometimes take 30+ seconds When you ask an AI system to do something complex — research a topic, create a document, solve a multi-step problem — and it takes 30 seconds or more to respond (much longer than a simple question), that delay is the agent loop in action. The system is making multiple tool calls, reading results, reasoning, calling more tools, checking its work — looping multiple times before delivering the final response. Each loop takes a few seconds (tool call + model inference). Five loops = the delay you're experiencing. It's not "slow" — it's doing genuine multi-step work.

entries.title: 15.1 — The Same Job Got Renamed Four Times
entries.summary: In 2023, someone got hired as a "prompt engineer." Their job: write really good instructions for AI systems. They got good at it. They learned all the tricks — chain-of-thought, few-shot examples, structured formatting. By 2025, their LinkedIn title changed to "context engineer" — same person, same desk, same company.…
entries.sourceText: In 2023, someone got hired as a "prompt engineer." Their job: write really good instructions for AI systems. They got good at it. They learned all the tricks — chain-of-thought, few-shot examples, structured formatting. By 2025, their LinkedIn title changed to "context engineer" — same person, same desk, same company. By mid-2026, they were calling themselves an "AI systems engineer." Their scope had expanded three times in three years, not because they'd changed careers but because the field kept zooming out. If you've been paying attention to AI since 2023, you've noticed this: the terminology keeps changing. It looks like hype churn. It isn't. Each term represents a genuine expansion of what the job actually involves. The craft got bigger, and each new name reflects a wider scope of responsibility. Here's the progression: Open the text version of this diagram 2023: PROMPT ENGINEERING → How you ask ↓ (zoom out) 2025: CONTEXT ENGINEERING → Everything it can see ↓ (zoom out) 2026: LOOP ENGINEERING → The cycle it runs in ↓ (zoom out) 2026: GRAPH ENGINEERING → The multi-agent system Each level includes everything below it. A graph engineer still writes prompts. They just also design loops, context systems, and multi-agent orchestrations. Let's look at each one. ⏸️ "But why did it keep expanding? Why wasn't prompt engineering enough?" Because each level hit a ceiling that only the next level could break through: Prompt engineering hit a wall when people realised: no matter how perfectly you phrase the question, if the model doesn't have the right information in its context window, the answer will be incomplete or hallucinated. You can't prompt your way to knowledge the model doesn't have access to. → Solution: control what the model sees , not just what you say . That's context engineering. Context engineering hit a wall when agents started doing multi-step tasks. You could assemble a perfect context window for one call — but an agent making 15 tool calls in sequence needs different information at each step. The context has to evolve as the task progresses. → Solution: design the cycle the agent runs in, including how context changes across iterations. That's loop engineering. Loop engineering hit a wall when tasks got too complex for one agent. A single agent trying to do research, check calendars, verify budgets, AND book a restaurant burns through its context window and loses coherence. → Solution: split into specialised agents that each handle one piece and hand off to each other. That's graph engineering. Each wall was real. Each zoom-out solved a problem the previous level couldn't. By the end of this chapter, you will be able to: Trace the evolution of AI engineering: prompt → context → loop → graph (2023–2026) Explain what each discipline actually means and what practitioners do day-to-day Understand why each is a "zoom-out" from the last Evaluate AI products more critically — when one works better than another, these layers are usually why Read AI articles from any period (2023–2026) without getting confused by shifting terminology Know where the field is today and what's likely next

entries.title: 15.2 — Prompt Engineering (2023): How You Ask
entries.summary: What it is: The craft of phrasing your instruction to the model in a way that produces good output. What practitioners do: Write clear, specific instructions Structure prompts with examples (few-shot) Test different phrasings to find what works Add constraints ("respond in JSON," "maximum 3 sentences") Use techniques like chain-of-thought ("think step by step") The scope: One message. One call.…
entries.sourceText: What it is: The craft of phrasing your instruction to the model in a way that produces good output. What practitioners do: Write clear, specific instructions Structure prompts with examples (few-shot) Test different phrasings to find what works Add constraints ("respond in JSON," "maximum 3 sentences") Use techniques like chain-of-thought ("think step by step") The scope: One message. One call. The prompt is the input, the response is the output. The practitioner's job is making that one exchange as good as possible. When it was the frontier: 2023 — when ChatGPT was new and the main skill was learning how to ask it for what you wanted effectively. Where it is now: Still essential — it's the foundation of everything above. But understood as just one piece of a larger system. Like knowing how to write a good sentence is essential for being a novelist, but being a novelist involves much more. Real example — booking a team dinner: At the prompt engineering level, you'd carefully write: Find me an Italian restaurant near downtown Vancouver that's good for groups of 8, available this Friday at 7pm, with a private dining option. Budget: $50-80 per person. That's it. One prompt, one response, one shot. The skill is making that single instruction as clear and specific as possible so the model gives you a useful answer on the first try. 💡 As we go through each level, watch how the same task — booking a team dinner — gets handled with progressively more sophisticated engineering. The task doesn't change. The system around it does.

entries.title: 15.3 — Context Engineering (mid-2025): Everything It Can See
entries.summary: What it is: Designing the complete context window — not just the prompt, but everything the model can access when it generates a response. The shift: People realised that the quality of AI output depends less on how you phrase the question and more on what information the model has access to when answering. The prompt matters, but it's maybe 10% of what determines output quality. The other 90% is: what documents were retrieved?…
entries.sourceText: What it is: Designing the complete context window — not just the prompt, but everything the model can access when it generates a response. The shift: People realised that the quality of AI output depends less on how you phrase the question and more on what information the model has access to when answering. The prompt matters, but it's maybe 10% of what determines output quality. The other 90% is: what documents were retrieved? What system instructions are loaded? What conversation history is retained? What tools are available? Real example — booking a team dinner (context engineering level): Same prompt as before. But now watch what happens before the model ever sees your words: Your message arrives at the system. The retrieval layer fires: it searches your company's HR database for your team's dietary restrictions. Finds: "Priya is vegan. Marcus is gluten-free." It queries your calendar history for past team dinners. Finds: "Last 3 dinners were at Italian restaurants rated 4+ on the post-dinner Slack poll." It pulls the expense policy document. Finds: "$80/person max for team dinners, pre-approval required for groups over 6." It checks the current date, your office location (downtown Vancouver), and your team's current roster (8 people). All of this gets assembled into the context window — along with your original prompt — as a single combined input. The model sees everything at once. The prompt didn't change. But the model's answer is dramatically better because it knows more when it answers. The skill isn't in the question — it's in what you assembled around the question before the model saw it. ⏸️ "Wait — so the context engineer's job is mostly happening BEFORE the model runs?" Yes. By the time the model generates a response, the context engineer's work is done. They designed the retrieval logic, chose which databases to query, decided what gets priority when the window is too full, and built the assembly pipeline. The model just processes whatever landed in the window. If the right information is there, the response is great. If it's missing, no amount of model intelligence helps. This is why Tobi Lütke called it "the real skill" — you're engineering the inputs , not the model itself. What practitioners do: Design RAG pipelines (what gets retrieved and how) Write system prompts that shape behaviour across all interactions Decide what goes into the context window and what gets left out Manage context window budgets (you can't fit everything — what's most important?) Design memory systems (what gets stored, what gets re-injected when) Choose chunking strategies for documents Optimise embedding models for retrieval quality The scope: Not one message — the entire context window assembly for every request. Key insight (Tobi Lütke, Shopify CEO, June 2025): "I really like the term 'context engineering' over prompt engineering… the art of providing all the context for the task to be plausibly solvable by the LLM." The real skill isn't writing a clever prompt — it's ensuring the model has the right information available when it needs to answer.

entries.title: 15.4 — Loop Engineering (June 2026): The Cycle It Runs In
entries.summary: What it is: Designing the execution cycle an agent runs in — not just what it sees, but how it iterates. The shift: Once agents started running in loops (Chapter 14) — perceive, reason, act, observe, repeat — a new set of design decisions emerged. Real example — booking a team dinner (loop engineering level): Now it's not one call and one answer.…
entries.sourceText: What it is: Designing the execution cycle an agent runs in — not just what it sees, but how it iterates. The shift: Once agents started running in loops (Chapter 14) — perceive, reason, act, observe, repeat — a new set of design decisions emerged. Real example — booking a team dinner (loop engineering level): Now it's not one call and one answer. It's an agent running a loop: Search for Italian restaurants near downtown Vancouver → gets 12 results Filter by group size (8+) and private dining → narrows to 4 Check availability for this Friday at 7pm → 2 are available Cross-check against team's dietary restrictions → 1 has vegan options Check price range against expense policy → within budget Present two final options to you → waits for your choice Books the reservation Loop engineering is designing that cycle : How many steps is it allowed? What if step 3 returns no availability — does it try Saturday, or try non-Italian restaurants? What if the booking tool fails? When should it ask you for clarification vs making a decision itself? What's the token budget for this whole task? ⏸️ "But what is the loop engineer actually DECIDING? What does their work product look like?" What a loop engineer specifies for the restaurant-booking agent. This is literally the configuration they write — you don't need to read every line, but notice how much of it is about handling what goes wrong : Open the text version of this diagram LOOP CONFIGURATION: Team Dinner Booking ───────────────────────────────────────── Max iterations: 12 Token budget: 50,000 (≈ $0.15) Timeout: 90 seconds STOPPING CONDITIONS: ✓ Reservation confirmed → DONE ✓ User says "cancel" → ABORT ✓ 12 iterations reached → ESCALATE to human ✓ All restaurants unavailable → WIDEN (try Saturday) ERROR RECOVERY: Tool timeout → retry once, then skip that restaurant Booking API down → present options, ask user to book manually Calendar API down → ask user for availability verbally ESCALATION TRIGGERS: Budget exceeded → ask user before proceeding Dietary conflict (no restaurant satisfies everyone) → present trade-offs Ambiguity ("Friday" = this Friday or next?) → ask user That's the loop engineer's deliverable. Not prose — a specification for how the agent handles every branch, failure, and edge case in its execution cycle. Without this, the agent either loops forever, gives up too early, or silently makes bad decisions. What practitioners do: Design stopping conditions (when has the agent done enough?) Set iteration caps (maximum 10 loops before escalating to human) Build feedback mechanisms (how does the agent evaluate its own progress?) Design error recovery (what happens when a tool call fails?) Set budget limits (maximum $X in inference costs per task) Create escalation paths (when should the agent ask for help?) Tune the balance between thoroughness and speed The scope: Not one message, not one context window — the entire iterative cycle an agent runs over a task. Coined by: Addy Osmani (Google), June 2026, in a widely-shared post that articulated the distinction: "Context engineering is what it knows. Loop engineering is what it does with what it knows, over time."

entries.summary: 📼 Rewind it: A multi-agent graph is closer to an old-school phone tree than a crowded group chat: each handoff has a named destination and a condition for what happens next. entries.sourceText: 📼 Rewind it: A multi-agent graph is closer to an old-school phone tree than a crowded group chat: each handoff has a named destination and a condition for what happens next. Software still needs checks for a message that is dropped, repeated, or sent down the wrong branch. What it is: Wiring multiple agents and loops into an orchestrated system — designing how they connect, hand off, share state, and coordinate. The shift: Once you have multiple agents (Chapter 14), you need to design how they work together. Real example — booking a team dinner (graph engineering level): Now it's not one agent running one loop. It's multiple specialised agents working in parallel: Scheduling Agent checks everyone's calendars and finds available times Restaurant Agent searches restaurants, checks menus, verifies dietary compliance Budget Agent validates against expense policy and processes pre-authorisation Booking Agent makes the actual reservation once the others agree Communications Agent drafts a message to the team with details A coordinator manages the handoffs: Scheduling Agent finds Friday 7pm works → passes to Restaurant Agent → passes shortlist to Budget Agent → passes approved options to you → your choice goes to Booking Agent → confirmation goes to Communications Agent. Graph engineering is designing that entire network : which agents exist, what each one does, how they pass work to each other, what happens when one fails, and how the whole system recovers from partial results. What actually happens when one agent in the graph fails: Let's say the Scheduling Agent checks calendars and finds: nobody is free Friday. What the graph does — mechanically, step by step: Scheduling Agent returns: {status: "no_availability", tried: "Friday 7pm", all_conflicts: ["Priya: kid's concert", "Marcus: flight"]} The coordinator receives this. It checks the graph's recovery rules. Recovery rule says: "If no availability on requested day → Scheduling Agent retries with ±1 day." Scheduling Agent runs again. Finds: Thursday 7pm works for 7/8 people (Marcus still flying). Coordinator checks quorum rule: "7/8 is above the 75% threshold → proceed." Coordinator passes Thursday 7pm to Restaurant Agent and Budget Agent (in parallel — they don't depend on each other). Both return results. Coordinator assembles the combined state and passes to the user for final approval. Total elapsed time: ~8 seconds. Total inference cost: ~$0.40 across all agents. What the user saw: "Friday didn't work for everyone — Thursday 7pm works for 7 of 8 (Marcus is travelling). Here are two restaurant options within budget. Want me to book?" The user never saw the failure, the retry, the parallel calls, or the quorum logic. They just got a smart result. That's graph engineering working. What practitioners do: Design the graph topology (which agents connect to which) Define handoff protocols (how Agent A passes work to Agent B) Manage shared state (information both agents need access to) Design parallel execution (which agents can run simultaneously) Build verification nodes (agents that check other agents' work) Handle failures (what happens when one node in the graph fails?) Optimise for latency and cost (the whole graph, not just individual agents) The scope: Not one agent, not one loop — the entire multi-agent system working together across potentially hundreds of steps. Where we are (August 2026): Graph engineering is the newest discipline. Only a handful of teams are working at this level — mostly at model labs and large technology companies. But as multi-agent systems become more common, this will become the standard way complex AI applications are built.

When a 2025 article says "prompt engineering is dead, context engineering is everything," that's describing the zoom-out. When a 2026 article introduces "loop" or "graph" engineering — it's the next zoom-out. None of them are wrong for their time. They're describing an expanding scope. entries.title: 16.1 — Why Regular Computers Can't Do This
entries.summary: In 2012, the team that won the ImageNet competition (Chapter 2's landmark moment) trained their network on two NVIDIA GTX 580 graphics cards — gaming GPUs, the kind you'd buy to play Call of Duty. entries.sourceText: In 2012, the team that won the ImageNet competition (Chapter 2's landmark moment) trained their network on two NVIDIA GTX 580 graphics cards — gaming GPUs, the kind you'd buy to play Call of Duty. Total hardware cost: about $1,000. Training time: roughly a week. By 2024, training a frontier model required 25,000 specialised GPUs running simultaneously for months. Total hardware cost: over $300 million. One company — NVIDIA — controlled about 80% of that market. Their stock price rose 800% in two years. How did gaming hardware become the most strategically important technology on Earth? And why can't you just use a normal computer? Your laptop has a CPU. It's brilliant at general tasks — running your browser, processing a spreadsheet, handling email. It works by doing one thing at a time, extremely fast, switching between tasks so quickly it appears to do everything simultaneously. AI doesn't need a processor that's brilliant at one thing at a time. It needs a processor that can do thousands of simple things at once. Remember training from Chapter 5: the model has billions of parameters (weights). During training, the system needs to: Multiply those billions of weights by incoming data Calculate how wrong the result was Adjust every weight slightly Do it again, millions of times Each individual calculation is simple — basic multiplication and addition. But there are billions of them, and they can mostly be done at the same time (they don't depend on each other's results). A CPU handles calculations like a single brilliant mathematician working one problem at a time: fast, but sequential. A GPU is like 10,000 average mathematicians working simultaneously: each one is slower, but together they finish the job far faster because the work is parallel. ⏸️ "But WHY can AI calculations be done in parallel? Why don't they depend on each other?" Think about a single layer in a neural network (Chapter 5). It has, say, 10,000 neurons. Each neuron takes the same input, multiplies it by its own weight, and produces its own output. Neuron 1 doesn't need to wait for Neuron 2's answer — they're all doing their own independent multiplication at the same time. That's one layer, one step: 10,000 independent multiplications. A real model has hundreds of layers, each with millions of neurons. During the forward pass, within each layer, all those multiplications happen simultaneously. Then the results pass to the next layer, and the next set of millions of multiplications happen simultaneously. It's like a factory assembly line where each station has 10,000 workers all doing the same task at once, then passing to the next station. A CPU would be one worker running between all 10,000 positions. A GPU gives you all 10,000 workers at once. Real numbers: A modern GPU like NVIDIA's H100 has 16,896 "cores" — 16,896 tiny processors each doing a multiplication simultaneously. That's why a single GPU can handle trillions of floating-point operations per second while a CPU with 8-16 cores cannot come close. 🔍 Concept in Practice: What ONE training step looks like across a GPU cluster You're training a frontier model. You have 4,000 H100 GPUs. What happens in a single training step — one pass through one batch of data: Data distributed. A batch of training examples (say, 4,096 text sequences) is split across the 4,000 GPUs. Each GPU gets a portion. Forward pass. Each GPU runs its portion of the data through its portion of the model (the model is too large for one GPU — it's split across groups of 8). Within each GPU, 16,896 cores fire simultaneously, doing matrix multiplications. Time: ~200ms. Power: 4,000 × 700W = 2.8 megawatts for this step. Loss calculated. Each GPU computes how wrong its predictions were (the loss function from Chapter 5). Results are numbers — tiny error signals for each parameter. Gradients communicated. Here's the expensive part: every GPU needs to share its error signals with every other GPU so they can all update in the same direction. 4,000 GPUs exchange data over NVLink and InfiniBand networking. Terabytes move between chips. This networking step is often the bottleneck — not the computation itself. Weights updated. All GPUs apply the averaged gradient to their portion of the model's weights. Every parameter shifts slightly. One step done. Repeat. Next batch. Same process. Millions of times over weeks to months. One step consumed: ~200ms of time, ~0.15 kWh of electricity (enough to run a microwave for 9 minutes), and generated enough heat to warm a small room. Multiply by millions of steps and you understand why training costs $100M+. By the end of this chapter, you will be able to: Explain why AI needs specialised chips (not regular computer processors) Describe the difference between CPUs, GPUs, and TPUs — and why GPUs dominate AI Understand why NVIDIA controls ~80% of the AI chip market and what "CUDA lock-in" means Explain what makes AI compute so expensive (and what's changing) Understand the concept of "parallel processing" and why it matters for AI

entries.title: 16.2 — GPUs: The Accidental AI Chip
entries.summary: GPUs were designed for video games. Rendering a 3D scene means calculating the colour and brightness of millions of pixels simultaneously — the same "thousands of simple parallel calculations" pattern that AI training requires. When researchers in the early 2010s realised that the maths of training neural networks looked almost identical to the maths of rendering graphics, GPUs became the default hardware for AI.…
entries.sourceText: GPUs were designed for video games. Rendering a 3D scene means calculating the colour and brightness of millions of pixels simultaneously — the same "thousands of simple parallel calculations" pattern that AI training requires. When researchers in the early 2010s realised that the maths of training neural networks looked almost identical to the maths of rendering graphics, GPUs became the default hardware for AI. The key insight: Nobody designed GPUs for AI. They just happened to be perfect for it. The architecture that makes 3D gaming smooth (massive parallelism, high memory bandwidth) is the same architecture that makes training a neural network fast.

entries.title: 16.3 — NVIDIA's Dominance (and Why It Persists)
entries.summary: In January 2023, NVIDIA was a well-known but not spectacular company — market cap around $360 billion, primarily thought of as a gaming chip maker. By June 2025, it briefly became the most valuable company on Earth, passing Apple and Microsoft. In two and a half years, its value grew more than 8×. What happened wasn't that NVIDIA suddenly got better.…
entries.sourceText: In January 2023, NVIDIA was a well-known but not spectacular company — market cap around $360 billion, primarily thought of as a gaming chip maker. By June 2025, it briefly became the most valuable company on Earth, passing Apple and Microsoft. In two and a half years, its value grew more than 8×. What happened wasn't that NVIDIA suddenly got better. What happened was that everyone else suddenly needed what NVIDIA had been building for 17 years. NVIDIA controls approximately 80% of the AI chip market (2026). Their data centre GPU revenue hit $62.3 billion in a single quarter. One company, making one category of product, accounting for most of the physical infrastructure that modern AI runs on. How? 1. They started 17 years early. In 2006, NVIDIA released CUDA — a programming language that lets developers talk directly to NVIDIA's chips. At the time, this seemed niche. But over the next 17 years, every major AI research lab built their tools, tutorials, code examples, and workflows on CUDA. By the time AI exploded in 2022, switching away from NVIDIA meant rewriting a decade of code. The moat isn't the chip — it's the software ecosystem built on top of it. This is called "CUDA lock-in," and it's one of the strongest competitive advantages in technology. 2. Each generation leapfrogs the last. The B200 (Blackwell architecture, 2024) delivers approximately 2.2× the training speed of the previous H100. The upcoming Vera Rubin architecture (2027) promises another leap. Every time a competitor starts to close the gap, NVIDIA releases a new generation and re-opens it. 3. They sell the whole stack, not just chips. NVIDIA doesn't just make GPUs — they sell the networking that connects thousands of GPUs together (NVLink), the software libraries that make them fast (cuDNN, TensorRT), and complete data centre solutions. Competing with NVIDIA means competing on chips AND networking AND software AND developer tools AND customer relationships, simultaneously. Nobody has managed all four. The numbers (2026): GPU Released Training throughput Price (approx.) A100 2020 Baseline ~$10,000 H100 2022 ~3× A100 ~$25,000–40,000 H200 2024 ~1.9× H100 (inference) ~$25,000–35,000 B200 (Blackwell) 2024 ~2.2× H100 (training) ~$30,000–40,000

entries.title: 16.4 — The Competitors: TPUs, Trainium, and Custom Silicon
entries.summary: NVIDIA isn't the only option — and the alternatives are growing: Google TPUs (Tensor Processing Units): Custom-designed chips built specifically for AI (not repurposed from graphics) Optimised for "tensor operations" (the core maths of neural networks) Used internally by Google for training Gemini and other models Available to external customers via Google Cloud Latest generation: Ironwood (2026) Advantage: lower training cost-per-FLOP…
entries.sourceText: NVIDIA isn't the only option — and the alternatives are growing: Google TPUs (Tensor Processing Units): Custom-designed chips built specifically for AI (not repurposed from graphics) Optimised for "tensor operations" (the core maths of neural networks) Used internally by Google for training Gemini and other models Available to external customers via Google Cloud Latest generation: Ironwood (2026) Advantage: lower training cost-per-FLOP than GPUs for Google's specific workloads Amazon Trainium: Amazon's custom AI chip, designed specifically for training Used to train Amazon's own models Available via AWS (Amazon Web Services) at lower cost than equivalent GPU instances Designed to break NVIDIA dependency for Amazon's infrastructure Latest generation: Trainium2 (2025) AMD: Makes GPUs that compete with NVIDIA (MI300 series) Gaining market share but still far behind (~10-15%) Advantage: often cheaper than equivalent NVIDIA hardware The pattern: Every major cloud company (Google, Amazon, Microsoft) is designing custom AI chips to reduce dependence on NVIDIA. But NVIDIA's ecosystem advantage (CUDA, 17 years of software) keeps them dominant for now. What's honestly uncertain: Will NVIDIA's dominance last? The arguments cut both ways. The CUDA ecosystem is deep — millions of lines of research code, every ML framework optimised for it, 17 years of accumulated tooling. Switching costs are enormous. But custom chips are getting better fast, and the companies designing them (Google, Amazon) are also the companies buying the most GPUs — meaning they're both NVIDIA's biggest customers and its most motivated competitors. If TPUs or Trainium reach "good enough" performance at significantly lower cost, the lock-in could break faster than historical analogies (like Intel's x86 dominance) would suggest. Or it might hold for another decade. Nobody knows — and billions of dollars of infrastructure investment are riding on the answer. 💡 Why custom chips matter for cost A general-purpose GPU has to be good at lots of things (graphics, scientific computing, AI, crypto mining). A custom chip like a TPU can be designed for ONLY AI workloads — which means it can be more efficient (faster, less power, lower cost) for that specific task. The trade-off: it can't do anything else. This is why Google trains Gemini on TPUs rather than buying NVIDIA GPUs — for their specific workload, purpose-built is more cost-effective.

entries.sourceText: Training a frontier model costs hundreds of millions of dollars in compute alone. Why? 1. Scale of computation. Training a frontier model requires approximately 10²⁵ floating-point operations (or more). That's a number with 25 zeros. No single chip can do this — you need thousands of GPUs running for months. 2. The chips themselves. A single H100 costs ~$30,000. Training a frontier model requires thousands of them. A 10,000-GPU cluster costs $300 million in hardware alone. 3. Memory (VRAM). Larger models need more memory to hold all their parameters during training. The H100 has 80GB of VRAM; the H200 has 141GB. If a model doesn't fit in one GPU's memory, you split it across multiple GPUs — adding complexity and cost. 4. Electricity. A single H100 consumes about 700 watts under load. A 10,000-GPU cluster consumes 7 megawatts — enough to power approximately 5,000 homes. At commercial electricity rates, that's millions per month. 5. Cooling. Those chips generate enormous heat. Data centres need sophisticated cooling systems (increasingly liquid cooling for AI clusters). 6. Networking. Thousands of GPUs need to communicate constantly during training. The networking hardware (NVLink, InfiniBand) to connect them at sufficient speed is itself extremely expensive. Estimated training costs (2026): Model class Approximate training cost GPT-3 (2020) $4.6–12 million GPT-4 (2023) $78–100+ million Frontier models (2025–2026) $200 million – $1 billion+

Inference happens every time anyone uses the model — billions of This is why model efficiency matters so much: techniques like quantisation (Chapter 9 — reducing precision from 16-bit to 4-bit), smaller specialised models, and better hardware for inference all reduce the cost of serving every request. 🔍 Concept in Practice: Why AI subscriptions cost $20/month and still lose money Running inference on a frontier model costs real money per request. When you send a long conversation to a model, you're consuming GPU time, electricity, and memory on expensive hardware. The $20/month subscription price for consumer AI products is often below cost — companies subsidise it to grow the user base, betting they'll find ways to reduce inference costs over time. The hardware described in this chapter is what that $20 is actually paying for: a fraction of a fraction of a second on a $30,000 GPU in a data centre.

entries.sourceText: CPU General-purpose processor. Good at many things sequentially. Not efficient for AI's parallel workload. GPU Massively parallel processor (thousands of simple cores). Originally for graphics, now the default AI chip. NVIDIA dominates (~80% market share). TPU Google's purpose-built AI chip. Optimised specifically for tensor (matrix) operations. More efficient than GPUs for Google's specific workloads. CUDA NVIDIA's software ecosystem (released 2006). 17 years of developer tools, libraries, and frameworks built on it. The real source of NVIDIA's lock-in — switching means rewriting code, not just swapping chips. VRAM Memory on the GPU chip. Determines how large a model you can load. H100: 80GB, H200: 141GB. When a model doesn't fit, you split across multiple GPUs. Parallel processing Doing thousands of calculations simultaneously. Why GPUs beat CPUs for AI: neural network maths is mostly independent operations that don't need to wait for each other. Inference > Training (2026) The industry now spends more on serving models ($23.3B) than training them ($19B). Training happens once; inference happens billions of times per day. Check your understanding Question: Why are GPUs useful for AI training? Answer: They perform many similar calculations in parallel, which suits the matrix operations used by neural networks.

entries.title: 17.1 — What's Actually Inside
entries.summary: Every time you ask an AI a question, somewhere in the world a building full of machines uses enough electricity to power a small neighbourhood — for a fraction of a second — to answer you. entries.sourceText: Every time you ask an AI a question, somewhere in the world a building full of machines uses enough electricity to power a small neighbourhood — for a fraction of a second — to answer you. That building exists. It has an address. It uses real water for cooling, draws real power from a real grid, and generates real heat that has to go somewhere. "The cloud" is not a metaphor you're supposed to take literally. It's a marketing term for "someone else's very large, very expensive building." Let's go inside one. A data centre is a large building — or a campus of buildings — filled with rows of metal racks. Each rack holds servers. In an AI-focused data centre, those servers contain the GPUs from Chapter 16 — thousands of them, networked together. What you'd see if you walked through one: Rows of 2-metre (6.5-foot) tall metal racks, spaced evenly, stretching the length of a warehouse Thick bundles of fibre optic cables running overhead and under raised floors The constant hum of fans (or, increasingly, the quiet of liquid-cooled systems) Blinking status lights — thousands of them Security: biometric access, cameras, mantrap entries Outside: massive electrical transformers, backup diesel generators, cooling towers Scale: A single hyperscale AI data centre campus might contain 50,000–100,000 GPUs. Microsoft's planned clusters for training frontier models involve over 100,000 GPUs working together as a single system. Meta's AI infrastructure spans multiple campuses across the world. ⏸️ "So when I ask ChatGPT a question... it goes to one of these?" Yes. Here's the physical journey — every step your request takes through the real world: Your fingertip hits the key. Your device packetises the message and sends it over your Wi-Fi to your router. Your ISP routes it. The packets travel through fibre optic cables — possibly across an ocean — to the nearest point of presence for the AI provider's network. Elapsed: ~20ms. Load balancer receives it. A routing system at the data centre decides which GPU cluster has capacity. Your request is assigned to a specific server in a specific rack in a specific row. Tokenisation runs on a CPU. Your text is split into tokens (Chapter 4). This is lightweight — a standard processor handles it. Elapsed: ~25ms. Tokens hit the GPU cluster. Your tokens — plus the system prompt, conversation history, and any retrieved documents — flow into GPU memory. The prefill phase (Chapter 7) runs: all input tokens processed in parallel across thousands of GPU cores. The chip consumes 700 watts during this burst. Heat dissipates into the liquid cooling system. Elapsed: ~200ms. Decode begins. The GPU generates output tokens one at a time. Each token requires a forward pass through the network's billions of parameters. Each pass consumes electricity. Each pass generates heat. The first word appears on your screen. Tokens stream back. Each generated token is immediately packetised and sent back through the same route — data centre → fibre → ISP → your router → your screen. You see words appearing one by one. Elapsed: 1–3 seconds for the full response. Cleanup. The KV cache (Chapter 7) is held briefly in case you respond immediately, then released. The GPU's memory is freed for the next user's request. Total energy consumed by your one question: approximately 0.001–0.01 kWh — enough to power a LED lightbulb for 3–30 minutes. Multiply by billions of queries per day, and you understand Chapter 17's energy numbers. Every AI response you've ever received was generated by actual hardware, in an actual building, consuming actual energy, generating actual heat that had to be physically removed. By the end of this chapter, you will be able to: Describe what an AI data centre actually looks like and how it's structured Explain the scale of energy consumption (and why it's growing so fast) Understand the relationship between AI growth and electricity demand Explain cooling, water usage, and the physical challenges of running AI at scale Understand the current energy mix powering AI and what's changing (nuclear, renewables, gas) Place the environmental cost of AI in perspective without editorialising in either direction

entries.title: 17.2 — The Energy Numbers
entries.summary: Here's a way to feel the scale: data centres used approximately 485 TWh of electricity globally in 2025. That's enough to power roughly 45 million average US homes for a year — more than the entire country of France uses. entries.sourceText: Here's a way to feel the scale: data centres used approximately 485 TWh of electricity globally in 2025. That's enough to power roughly 45 million average US homes for a year — more than the entire country of France uses. It's about 1.5% of all electricity generated on Earth — from a category of building that most people have never seen or thought about. And that's the number before AI agents became mainstream. Where it's going (IEA, UN, multiple sources): Year Global data centre electricity For perspective 2025 ~485 TWh More than France 2030 (low estimate) ~600 TWh More than Germany 2030 (IEA central projection) ~945 TWh Approaching Japan US alone, 2030 400–600 TWh Would require dozens of new power plants Why it's growing this fast: A single AI inference query uses approximately 10× more electricity than a standard web search. Ask Google a question — a few servers look up an index and return results. Ask ChatGPT a question — thousands of GPU cores run billions of calculations to generate each word. And usage is skyrocketing: more people using AI, more complex tasks (agents that make 15 tool calls use 15× more compute than a simple Q&A), and larger models. The paradox (IEA, April 2026): "Power consumption per AI task is declining rapidly, with efficiency improving at a rate unprecedented in energy history. However, more people are using AI, and energy-intensive uses — such as AI agents — are on the rise." In other words: each query is getting cheaper, but the total number of queries is growing far faster than the efficiency gains. It's like cars getting better fuel economy while total miles driven triples — you still burn more fuel.

entries.title: 17.3 — Cooling: The Hidden Challenge
entries.summary: Chips generate heat. The more powerful the chip, the more heat. An H100 GPU consumes 700 watts and converts almost all of it to heat. Multiply by 10,000 GPUs in a cluster and you have 7 megawatts of heat that needs to go somewhere. Air cooling (traditional): Cold air is pushed through the server racks, absorbing heat, then exhausted and cooled again. Simple but increasingly insufficient for dense AI hardware.…
entries.sourceText: Chips generate heat. The more powerful the chip, the more heat. An H100 GPU consumes 700 watts and converts almost all of it to heat. Multiply by 10,000 GPUs in a cluster and you have 7 megawatts of heat that needs to go somewhere. Air cooling (traditional): Cold air is pushed through the server racks, absorbing heat, then exhausted and cooled again. Simple but increasingly insufficient for dense AI hardware. For efficient hyperscale centres, cooling accounts for about 7% of total electricity use. For less-efficient facilities, it can be over 30%. Liquid cooling (the trend): Liquid circulates through or directly contacts the hot chips, absorbing heat far more efficiently than air. Some systems use cold plates (liquid flows through a metal plate touching the chip); others use immersion (chips submerged directly in non-conductive liquid). Most new AI-focused data centres (2025+) are designed for liquid cooling from the start. Water usage: Cooling towers evaporate water to reject heat. A large data centre can use millions of litres of water per day. This is increasingly a constraint in drought-prone regions and a point of community concern when new centres are proposed.

entries.title: 17.4 — Where the Electricity Comes From
entries.summary: Current energy mix powering data centres globally (IEA): Renewables (wind, solar, hydro): ~27% Natural gas: ~26% Nuclear: ~15% Coal and other: remaining What's changing (2025–2026): Every major hyperscaler has announced plans to power AI data centres with cleaner energy: Nuclear: Multiple companies have signed deals to restart or build nuclear plants specifically for data centres.…
entries.sourceText: Current energy mix powering data centres globally (IEA): Renewables (wind, solar, hydro): ~27% Natural gas: ~26% Nuclear: ~15% Coal and other: remaining What's changing (2025–2026): Every major hyperscaler has announced plans to power AI data centres with cleaner energy: Nuclear: Multiple companies have signed deals to restart or build nuclear plants specifically for data centres. Microsoft signed a deal to restart Three Mile Island's Unit 1 reactor. Amazon purchased a nuclear-powered data centre campus. Small Modular Reactors (SMRs) are being developed specifically for data centre power. Renewables: Massive solar and wind farm contracts. Google claims to run on 100% renewable energy (via matching — they buy enough renewables to offset usage, though not all at the same hour). Natural gas: Still heavily used, especially for new capacity that needs to come online quickly (gas plants are faster to build than nuclear or large-scale renewables). The tension: AI companies have pledged net-zero or carbon-free targets. But AI electricity demand is growing so fast that their overall carbon footprints are increasing even as the percentage from renewables grows. Google's emissions rose 13% in 2023 and continued rising in 2024-2025, despite more renewable purchases — because total energy use grew faster.

But grid capacity there is increasingly strained. New AI centres are being built in places with available power: the Midwest US, Nordic countries, parts of Canada. 🔍 Concept in Practice: Why "the cloud" is actually very physical "The cloud" sounds ethereal — as if your data floats somewhere abstract. In reality, every AI query you make travels via fibre optic cables to a specific building in a specific location, is processed on a specific GPU that's consuming electricity and generating heat, and the result travels back. When cloud services go down (as they occasionally do), it's often because something physical happened: a power failure, a cooling system breakdown, a fibre cable cut. The "cloud" is a marketing term for "someone else's very large, very expensive computer building."

entries.sourceText: A modern AI chip is arguably the most complex manufactured object in human history. A single NVIDIA B200 GPU contains approximately 208 billion transistors — structures smaller than a virus — etched onto a piece of silicon the size of your thumbnail. No single company, and no single country, can make one alone. The supply chain spans the globe: The journey of an AI chip: Raw silicon — purified from sand (quartz) to 99.9999999% purity. Mostly from China, Russia, Brazil. Silicon wafers — sliced into thin discs at wafer manufacturers (Japan, Germany, US). Chip design — NVIDIA designs the chip architecture (California, US). This is intellectual property — the "blueprint." Lithography machines — ASML (Netherlands) builds the EUV machines that print the chip patterns. Only ASML can do this. Each machine costs ~$350 million. Manufacturing (fabrication) — TSMC (Taiwan) prints the design onto silicon wafers using ASML's machines. This is where the physical chip gets made. Memory — HBM (High Bandwidth Memory) is manufactured and stacked by Samsung and SK Hynix (South Korea). Packaging — The chip die is assembled with memory into a complete package. Advanced packaging is itself a bottleneck (TSMC, Taiwan + some in the US). Assembly into servers — Chips are mounted on boards, installed in server racks (various manufacturers globally). Deployment — Servers are installed in data centres (Chapter 17). Total time from sand to working GPU in a data centre: approximately 6–9 months. By the end of this chapter, you will be able to: Trace the journey of an AI chip from raw materials to data centre Explain why TSMC (one company in Taiwan) manufactures over 90% of the world's most advanced chips Understand the geopolitical significance of the AI supply chain Describe the major chokepoints and why disruption would be catastrophic Explain why countries are investing billions to build domestic chip manufacturing

entries.title: 18.2 — TSMC: The Single Most Important Factory
entries.summary: TSMC controls approximately 70% of global foundry revenue and over 90% of the world's most advanced chip production (3nm and 5nm nodes). They manufacture chips for NVIDIA, Apple, AMD, Qualcomm, and dozens of other companies. Why one company? entries.sourceText: TSMC controls approximately 70% of global foundry revenue and over 90% of the world's most advanced chip production (3nm and 5nm nodes). They manufacture chips for NVIDIA, Apple, AMD, Qualcomm, and dozens of other companies. Why one company? Chip manufacturing at leading-edge nodes is extraordinarily difficult and extraordinarily expensive: A single fab costs $10–20 billion to build It takes 3–5 years to build and bring online The manufacturing process involves thousands of precise steps Yield (the percentage of chips that work correctly) takes years to optimise TSMC has been doing this for 30+ years — the accumulated expertise is nearly impossible to replicate quickly ⏸️ "But if it's so important, why can't someone just build another one? Surely with enough money..." Here's why money isn't enough — told mechanically: Making a chip at 3nm (current leading edge) involves approximately 1,500 process steps. Each step must be perfect to within tolerances smaller than a single virus. If step 847 is off by a fraction, every chip in that batch is garbage. The knowledge of how to get all 1,500 steps right — in sequence, at volume, reliably — lives in TSMC's engineering workforce. It's not written down in a manual you can buy. It's embodied expertise: thousands of engineers who spent years learning how this specific machine behaves in this specific clean room with this specific chemical supplier's materials at this specific humidity level. Yield is the proof. When TSMC opens a new process node, their initial yield might be 30% — meaning 70% of chips come out broken. Over 12–18 months, through thousands of micro-adjustments (tweaking temperatures by fractions of a degree, adjusting chemical concentrations by parts-per-million, realigning lithography masks by nanometres), they push yield above 90%. That optimisation process is not transferable. It's learned by doing, on that specific equipment, in that specific facility. This is why Intel — a company with decades of chip manufacturing experience and enormous resources — has struggled to match TSMC's leading-edge production. And why TSMC's Arizona fab, within TSMC's planned $165 billion total US investment, is expected to produce at lower yield than Taiwan operations for years. You can copy a recipe. You can't copy 30 years of hands learning how the dough feels. The concentration risk: TSMC operates almost entirely from one island — Taiwan — located 160 km (100 miles) from mainland China. Bloomberg Economics estimates a full Taiwan conflict could cost approximately $10 trillion in first-year global economic impact.

entries.title: 18.3 — ASML: The Other Monopoly
entries.summary: If TSMC is the only company that can make the chips, ASML (Netherlands) is the only company that makes the machines TSMC uses to make them. And what ASML makes is arguably the most extraordinary engineering achievement in human history — a machine that uses light to print structures smaller than a virus, on a piece of silicon, billions of times, without error.…
entries.sourceText: If TSMC is the only company that can make the chips, ASML (Netherlands) is the only company that makes the machines TSMC uses to make them. And what ASML makes is arguably the most extraordinary engineering achievement in human history — a machine that uses light to print structures smaller than a virus, on a piece of silicon, billions of times, without error. What an ASML EUV lithography machine actually involves: A laser fires 50,000 times per second at tiny droplets of molten tin — each droplet about 25 micrometres wide (a quarter of the width of a human hair). Each hit vaporises the tin into a plasma that emits extreme ultraviolet light — light with a wavelength of 13.5 nanometres, so short that it's absorbed by air and even by glass. The light can't pass through lenses. Instead, it bounces off mirrors polished so perfectly that if one were scaled to the size of Germany, the tallest bump would be 1 millimetre high. The reflected light passes through a mask (the chip pattern) and prints the circuit design onto a silicon wafer below, at a resolution of a few nanometres. Structures smaller than individual virus particles. Billions of them per chip. Each machine: Costs approximately $350 million Weighs over 150 tonnes (~165,000 kg / 364,000 lbs) Contains 100,000+ components from 5,000+ suppliers across dozens of countries Is shipped in 40+ freight containers Takes months to install and calibrate on-site Requires its own dedicated team of ASML engineers to maintain No other company in the world can build these machines. Not because nobody's tried — Samsung, Intel, Canon, Nikon all attempted EUV lithography. ASML spent 20 years and tens of billions of dollars getting it to work. Everyone else gave up. ASML has a complete monopoly on EUV lithography — which is required for any chip at 7nm or below (i.e., all modern AI chips). Every AI response you've ever received — every ChatGPT answer, every Claude conversation, every Midjourney image — was generated on hardware that could only exist because of machines built by this one company in Veldhoven, Netherlands.

entries.sourceText: Since 2022, the United States has imposed escalating export controls preventing the sale of advanced AI chips (and the machines to make them) to China. This is one of the most significant technology restrictions in modern history. What's restricted: NVIDIA cannot sell its most advanced GPUs (H100, B200) to China ASML cannot sell EUV lithography machines to China Software tools used to design chips are restricted China's response: Investing heavily in domestic chip manufacturing (but still years behind on leading-edge) Imposing its own export controls on critical minerals (gallium, germanium) needed for chip production Developing alternative AI architectures that work on less-advanced chips The result: The global chip supply chain, which was built on decades of international cooperation and specialisation, is fragmenting along geopolitical lines. Countries are spending billions to build domestic manufacturing capacity — not because it's economically efficient, but because dependence on a single source is now seen as a national security risk. 💡 Why this matters for AI progress The speed of AI development is not limited only by algorithmic breakthroughs or research talent. It is physically constrained by how many advanced chips can be manufactured, how fast new fabs can be built, and whether the geopolitical conditions allow the supply chain to function. When people ask "how fast will AI advance?" — part of the answer is in factories in Taiwan and memory plants in South Korea.

TSMC says its planned total US investment is $165 billion, including expanded Arizona manufacturing and research facilities. Intel is expanding US manufacturing. EU Chips Act: €43 billion to double Europe's global chip production share. Japan: Attracting TSMC to build a fab in Kumamoto. India: Investing in chip packaging and assembly facilities. Taiwan's $250 billion deal (2026): Guaranteed credit for Taiwanese chip companies to expand US production capacity. The reality check: Even with these investments, leading-edge manufacturing outside Taiwan will remain limited for years. TSMC's Arizona fab is expected to produce chips by 2025-2026, but at smaller scale and (initially) lower yield than Taiwan operations. You cannot replicate 30 years of manufacturing expertise with money alone.

entries.title: 19.1 — The Roles
entries.summary: 📼 Rewind it: If you ever opened a CD booklet and found a page of tiny production credits, you saw the difference between the performer on the cover and everyone who made the album possible. AI products work the same way: the model may get the headline, but researchers, engineers, product teams, safety teams, infrastructure, and operators determine whether it is useful, safe, and available.…
entries.sourceText: 📼 Rewind it: If you ever opened a CD booklet and found a page of tiny production credits, you saw the difference between the performer on the cover and everyone who made the album possible. AI products work the same way: the model may get the headline, but researchers, engineers, product teams, safety teams, infrastructure, and operators determine whether it is useful, safe, and available. A job listing goes up in 2024: "Prompt Engineer — $250K–$350K." Requires: no specific degree. No coding experience necessary. "Ability to write clearly and think systematically." That's it. Two years later, the same role at the same company is called "AI Systems Architect" and now requires understanding of RAG pipelines, evaluation design, and multi-agent orchestration. Same desk. The job grew that fast. The AI industry has more job titles than it probably needs — and they change faster than any other field's ever have. Some are well-defined. Some overlap heavily. Some didn't exist eighteen months ago. Here's a clear map of who does what, right now — organised by what part of the system they touch. The Research Layer: Pushing the Frontier Research Scientist / AI Researcher What they do: Invent new architectures, training methods, and capabilities. Publish academic papers. Run experiments to advance the state of the art. Where they work: OpenAI, Anthropic, Google DeepMind, Meta FAIR, university labs. What they need: PhD (typically), deep maths and statistics, ability to read and produce academic work. What they produce: Papers, proofs of concept, new techniques that the rest of the industry then builds on. Example output: "Attention Is All You Need" (2017) — the paper that introduced the transformer architecture. The Building Layer: Making It Work Machine Learning Engineer (MLE) What they do: Take research concepts and build them into reliable, scalable production systems. They write the code that trains models, optimises performance, and deploys to users. Where they work: Everywhere AI is used — tech companies, startups, enterprises. What they need: Strong software engineering + ML knowledge. Python, PyTorch/TensorFlow, cloud platforms, system design. What they produce: Working models running in production. The actual system that serves your requests. Data Scientist What they do: Analyse data to answer business questions. Build predictive models for specific use cases (customer churn, fraud detection, demand forecasting). Focus on extracting insights. Where they work: Every industry — finance, retail, healthcare, marketing, logistics. What they need: Statistics, SQL, Python/R, visualisation tools, communication skills to explain findings. What they produce: Insights, dashboards, predictive models, A/B test analyses, recommendations. Data Engineer What they do: Build and maintain the infrastructure that moves data from where it's created to where it's needed. Design pipelines, ensure data quality, handle scale. Where they work: Anywhere with significant data — which is everywhere. What they need: SQL, distributed systems (Spark, Kafka), cloud platforms, understanding of data formats and storage. What they produce: Reliable data pipelines. If they do their job well, you never notice them — but if they don't, nothing else works. The Operations Layer: Keeping It Running MLOps Engineer What they do: Keep machine learning systems running in production. Handle deployment, monitoring, model versioning, retraining schedules, scaling. The "DevOps for ML." Where they work: Any company running ML in production. What they need: Software engineering, infrastructure skills, understanding of ML model lifecycle. What they produce: Reliable, monitored, scalable AI systems that don't break at 3am. Infrastructure Engineer / Platform Engineer What they do: Build and maintain the compute infrastructure — GPU clusters, networking, storage, cloud platforms. The hardware-software interface. Where they work: Cloud providers, large AI companies, any company running their own GPU infrastructure. What they need: Systems engineering, networking, hardware knowledge, distributed computing. What they produce: The platform everything else runs on. The Application Layer: Making It Useful AI/ML Product Manager What they do: Decide what to build, for whom, and why. Translate between user needs and technical capabilities. Prioritise features. Define success metrics. Where they work: Any company building AI products. What they need: Business acumen, technical literacy (don't need to code, but need to understand capabilities and limitations), user empathy. What they produce: Product strategy, roadmaps, feature specifications, launch decisions. Prompt Engineer / Context Engineer / AI Engineer What they do: Design the instructions, system prompts, RAG pipelines, and evaluation suites that make AI systems work well for specific tasks. Evolved from "prompt engineering" to the broader role described in Chapter 15. Where they work: AI companies, enterprises deploying AI, consulting firms. What they need: Deep understanding of how models work (without necessarily building them), excellent writing, systematic testing mindset, evaluation design. What they produce: System prompts, evaluation suites, RAG configurations, workflow designs. Note: This role barely existed before 2023 and has evolved faster than almost any other job title in history. AI Solutions Architect What they do: Design the overall system architecture for AI deployments — which models, which infrastructure, how pieces connect, what trade-offs to make. Where they work: Cloud providers, consulting firms, enterprise AI teams. What they need: Broad technical knowledge (models, infrastructure, security, cost), communication skills. What they produce: Architecture designs, vendor recommendations, deployment plans. The Governance Layer: Keeping It Safe AI Ethics Researcher / Responsible AI Lead What they do: Study the societal impacts of AI systems. Design fairness metrics, audit for bias, develop governance frameworks. Where they work: Large AI companies, academic institutions, government, NGOs. What they need: Interdisciplinary background (philosophy, law, social science + technical literacy). What they produce: Fairness audits, policy recommendations, governance frameworks, bias detection tools. AI Safety Researcher What they do: Work on preventing AI systems from causing harm — alignment research (making models follow human intent), red-teaming (adversarial testing), interpretability (understanding what models are doing internally). Where they work: Anthropic, OpenAI, DeepMind, academic labs. What they need: Strong ML background + orientation toward risk and safety. What they produce: Safety evaluations, alignment techniques, interpretability tools, guardrail systems. ⏸️ "OK — but how do these roles actually connect? Who hands off to whom?" Let's trace one real task through the chain. A company wants to add a "summarise this document" feature to their product. Step 1: Product Manager decides the feature is worth building. Writes a spec: "User uploads a PDF, gets a 3-paragraph summary in 10 seconds. Must work for documents up to 50 pages. Must not hallucinate facts not in the document." Step 2: ML Engineer chooses the model (Claude 3.5 Sonnet — fast enough for 10-second latency, good at summarisation), designs the serving architecture (how the PDF gets chunked if it's too long for the context window), and builds the inference pipeline. Step 3: Data Engineer builds the pipeline that converts uploaded PDFs into text the model can process — handling OCR for scanned documents, stripping formatting, chunking pages. Step 4: Context/Prompt Engineer writes the system prompt ("Summarise the following document in exactly 3 paragraphs. Include only information explicitly stated in the document. If the document is unclear, say so."), designs the chunking strategy for long documents, and builds the eval suite (50 test documents with known-good summaries to compare against). Step 5: Safety/Red Team tests: can users trick it into ignoring the document and summarising something else? Does it hallucinate when the document is ambiguous? Does it leak content from other users' documents? Step 6: MLOps Engineer deploys to production, sets up monitoring (latency tracking, error rates, cost per request), builds the auto-scaling so it handles 10 users or 10,000 without breaking. Step 7: Product Manager (again) reviews user feedback after launch. "Summaries are too generic." Back to Step 4 — the prompt engineer adjusts the instructions and re-runs evals. Total elapsed time: 3–6 weeks from spec to launch. The point: no single role does this alone. Each person's output becomes the next person's input. The PDF text the data engineer produces feeds into the context window the prompt engineer designs. The eval suite the prompt engineer builds is what the MLOps engineer runs after every model update. The chain only works because each person understands what the person before them produced and what the person after them needs. By the end of this chapter, you will be able to: Name the major job titles in the AI industry and explain what each one actually does Distinguish between roles that build AI systems, roles that deploy them, and roles that govern them Understand how job titles have evolved (and why some are confusing) Know what skills each role requires — and which roles are new (didn't exist before 2020) Read AI job postings and company org charts without confusion

entries.summary: Behind the high-profile roles, there's a massive workforce that doesn't get headlines: Data labellers / Annotators: The people who label training data — tagging images, rating model outputs, providing the human judgments that RLHF and DPO (Chapter 9) depend on. entries.sourceText: Behind the high-profile roles, there's a massive workforce that doesn't get headlines: Data labellers / Annotators: The people who label training data — tagging images, rating model outputs, providing the human judgments that RLHF and DPO (Chapter 9) depend on. Hundreds of thousands of people globally. Historically gig workers at low pay; evolving toward more specialised, better-compensated expert annotators as quality requirements increase. These roles exist at companies like Scale AI, Surge AI, and Sama — and are often outsourced to workers in the Philippines, Kenya, India, and other countries. This is the human labour that makes "artificial" intelligence possible. 🔍 Concept in Practice: Why the same person has three different job titles on LinkedIn A real person's LinkedIn might say "AI Engineer" in 2024, "Context Engineer" in 2025, and "AI Systems Architect" in 2026 — same person, same company, same desk. They didn't change jobs. The scope of their job expanded (Chapter 15's zoom-out), and the industry invented new titles to describe the wider scope. When you see unfamiliar AI job titles, ask: "Which part of the system does this person touch?" That question always has a clear answer, even when the title is vague.
