entries.sourceText: A few patterns that help decode job titles and company structures: "Engineer" vs "Scientist": Engineers build things that work. Scientists discover new things. The boundary is blurry — many people do both — but if a title says "engineer," the emphasis is on building reliable systems. If it says "scientist" or "researcher," the emphasis is on discovery and experimentation. "ML" vs "AI" vs "Data": Often used interchangeably in job titles. Roughly: "Data" roles focus on data itself (cleaning, moving, analysing). "ML" roles focus on building models. "AI" is increasingly used as the umbrella term for any role touching these systems. The seniority ladder: Junior → Mid → Senior → Staff → Principal → Distinguished. At most companies, "Staff" and above means you're setting direction for teams and systems, not just building individual components. 🔍 Concept in Practice: Why your company's "AI team" might be 3 people or 300 The range of roles described above represents the full ecosystem. A startup might have one person wearing five hats: designing prompts, building pipelines, running evals, deploying to production. A large technology company might have separate teams for each role — hundreds of people across research, engineering, operations, product, safety, and governance. Neither is wrong — the size of the team reflects the scale and complexity of what they're building.

entries.title: Chapter 20: AGI, ASI, and the Frontier
entries.summary: The general idea: An AI system that can match or exceed human cognitive ability across any intellectual task — not just one narrow domain, but the full range of things humans can think about and do. entries.title: 20.1 — What Is AGI? (And Why No One Agrees)
entries.summary: The general idea: An AI system that can match or exceed human cognitive ability across any intellectual task — not just one narrow domain, but the full range of things humans can think about and do. Why the definition is contested: Everyone agrees current AI is narrow: ChatGPT is impressive at language but can't independently conduct scientific research, navigate a new city, or handle the full complexity of a human job without help.…
entries.sourceText: The general idea: An AI system that can match or exceed human cognitive ability across any intellectual task — not just one narrow domain, but the full range of things humans can think about and do. Why the definition is contested: Everyone agrees current AI is narrow: ChatGPT is impressive at language but can't independently conduct scientific research, navigate a new city, or handle the full complexity of a human job without help. "AGI" is the point where that changes — where the system can do anything a human can, at least as well. But what exactly counts? Does it need a body? Emotions? Social intelligence? Does "as good as a human" mean "average human" or "best human in each domain"? Does it need to learn new tasks as quickly as humans? Different definitions from different people (2025–2026): OpenAI–Microsoft contractual process: OpenAI may declare AGI, with that declaration verified by an independent expert panel. Their public agreement does not publish a simple capability threshold, which is another reminder that organisations operationalise the term differently. Sam Altman (OpenAI CEO): AGI could be reached "in the next four or five years" (stated 2024) Dario Amodei (Anthropic CEO): "Human-level AI" in two to three years. Prefers the term "powerful AI" over "AGI" because AGI is overhyped Demis Hassabis (Google DeepMind CEO): Possibly a decade away Jensen Huang (NVIDIA CEO, March 2026): "We've achieved AGI" — but his definition is narrower than most Yann LeCun (Meta Chief AI Scientist): Current approaches (LLMs) won't get us there. Fundamentally new architectures needed. Decades away. There are as many estimates of when AGI will arrive as there are people working in the field. And to complicate matters further, there is disagreement on what AGI even is. This isn't unusual — it's what you'd expect for a concept that's never existed before. By the end of this chapter, you will be able to: Define AGI and ASI — what they mean and where the definitions disagree Understand why experts disagree so profoundly on timelines (months vs decades) Explain why this disagreement isn't just academic — it drives real decisions about safety, regulation, and investment Separate the hype from what's actually known Hold multiple possibilities in mind without needing to pick a side

entries.sourceText: Term Plain English AGI (Artificial General Intelligence) An AI system that can perform any intellectual task a human can — not just one specialised skill, but the full range of reasoning, learning, and problem-solving across all domains ASI (Artificial Superintelligence) A hypothetical AI that significantly exceeds the best human intelligence in every domain — science, strategy, creativity, social skills Narrow AI / ANI What we have today. AI that's excellent at specific tasks but can't generalise. A chess AI can't write poetry. A language model can't play chess at superhuman levels (without tools). Alignment The problem of ensuring a highly capable AI system actually does what humans want and intend Scaling hypothesis The idea that current architectures (transformers) will reach AGI if we simply make them bigger with more data and compute Emergence Capabilities that appear unexpectedly as models get larger — abilities no one programmed in

entries.title: 20.2 — What Would AGI Actually Mean?
entries.summary: If a system could genuinely match human-level intelligence across all domains: What it could do — concretely, mechanically, not abstractly: Imagine giving a system a task it has never been trained on, in a domain nobody anticipated. Something like: "This factory's widget rejection rate spiked from 2% to 8% last Tuesday.…
entries.sourceText: If a system could genuinely match human-level intelligence across all domains: What it could do — concretely, mechanically, not abstractly: Imagine giving a system a task it has never been trained on, in a domain nobody anticipated. Something like: "This factory's widget rejection rate spiked from 2% to 8% last Tuesday. Figure out why and fix it." An AGI system would need to: Understand the problem without being told what a widget is, what the factory makes, or what "rejection rate" means in this context — figure it out from available information. Decide what data to gather — ask for sensor logs, quality control reports, maintenance schedules, shift rosters, raw material shipment records. Nobody tells it which sources matter. Form hypotheses — "Was it a raw material batch change? A calibration drift? A new operator on the night shift? A temperature fluctuation?" Design tests to distinguish between hypotheses — "If it's the material batch, rejections should correlate with shipment #4472. If it's calibration drift, rejections should increase gradually, not spike." Revise its thinking when evidence contradicts its hypothesis — abandon wrong paths without being told they're wrong. Propose a fix — and predict its consequences correctly. Current systems (2026) can do pieces of this — especially when given clear instructions and the right tools. What they can't do is the full chain autonomously, in a novel domain, without specific training or scaffolding for that domain. That gap — from "can do pieces with help" to "can do the whole thing cold" — is what separates current AI from AGI. No one agrees on how wide that gap is. What changes: Most intellectual work could, in theory, be done by AI systems Scientific progress could accelerate dramatically Economic structures that depend on human cognitive labour would be fundamentally disrupted The alignment problem (Chapter 11) becomes existential rather than merely important

Not just as good as a smart human — vastly, incomprehensibly better. entries.sourceText: Artificial Superintelligence is the hypothetical stage beyond AGI — a system that exceeds the best human intelligence in every domain by a significant margin. Not just as good as a smart human — vastly, incomprehensibly better. Why people take it seriously: If an AGI system can do AI research itself, it could potentially improve itself Self-improvement could compound — each better version builds an even better next version This could lead to a rapid capability explosion ("intelligence explosion") Why others are sceptical: We don't know if intelligence can scale that way Physical constraints (compute, energy, data) may impose hard limits "Intelligence" may not be one thing that can simply be "turned up" Self-improvement may hit diminishing returns quickly Nobody knows. This is genuine uncertainty, not evasion. The smartest people in the field disagree profoundly.

entries.title: 20.4 — The Two Big Camps (2026)
entries.summary: The AI community is broadly split on timelines: Camp 1: "Sooner than you think" (months to years) Current scaling is working. Models are getting more capable with more compute. Emergent capabilities keep appearing unexpectedly as models scale. We're on a trajectory that could reach AGI-level performance by 2027–2030. The architecture doesn't need to be fundamentally different — transformers + scale + better data + tools might be enough.…
entries.sourceText: The AI community is broadly split on timelines: Camp 1: "Sooner than you think" (months to years) Current scaling is working. Models are getting more capable with more compute. Emergent capabilities keep appearing unexpectedly as models scale. We're on a trajectory that could reach AGI-level performance by 2027–2030. The architecture doesn't need to be fundamentally different — transformers + scale + better data + tools might be enough. Key voices: Altman, Amodei, many at OpenAI and Anthropic Camp 2: "Fundamentally new approaches needed" (decade+) LLMs are impressive but they don't truly "understand" — they predict tokens. Current systems lack grounding, embodiment, causal reasoning, and true planning. What looks like intelligence is sophisticated pattern matching, not general intelligence. We need new architectures, not just bigger versions of current ones. Key voices: LeCun, Hassabis (partially), many academic researchers ⏸️ "But what does 'emergence' actually look like? Can you show me?" Here's a real example. When GPT-3 was being trained (2020), the researchers gave it a simple task: translate English to French. At 1 billion parameters, it could barely manage basic phrases. At 10 billion, it was passable. Then somewhere between 100 billion and 175 billion parameters — with NO change to the training method, NO translation-specific training, NO new data — it became surprisingly competent at translation. Nobody added that capability. It emerged from scale. More striking: chain-of-thought reasoning. Small models told "think step by step" just produce gibberish reasoning. Models above a certain size (~100B parameters) suddenly produce coherent step-by-step reasoning that actually leads to correct answers on math problems. Below that threshold: nothing. Above it: the capability appears, seemingly from nowhere. Why this is unsettling: Nobody designed these capabilities in. Nobody predicted the specific threshold where they'd appear. The training process was identical at every scale — the only variable was size . It's as if you were building taller and taller towers of Lego, and at a certain height, the tower spontaneously started generating electricity. You didn't add a generator. The electricity emerged from the structure. Why sceptics push back: Maybe it's not "emergence" — maybe it's a measurement artefact. If you test with finer-grained benchmarks instead of pass/fail thresholds, the capabilities improve gradually rather than appearing suddenly. The debate is real and unresolved. Where the evidence points (August 2026): Capabilities continue to grow faster than most predicted But genuine understanding and reliability remain elusive Models still hallucinate, still fail at novel situations, still require extensive scaffolding The "last mile" from "impressive" to "reliable" is proving difficult

entries.sourceText: The AGI timeline question isn't philosophical abstraction. It drives real decisions: If AGI is 2–5 years away: Safety research is urgent (we might not have time to solve alignment before it arrives) Economic disruption planning needs to start now Regulation can't wait for the technology to settle The companies building it have enormous responsibility and very little time If AGI is 10–30 years away: We have time to do safety research carefully Current AI is powerful but manageable — focus on near-term deployment issues The hype cycle may produce a crash before AGI arrives Over-regulating now might be premature If current architectures can't reach AGI at all: We're optimising a tool, not approaching a transformation Economic impacts are real but incremental Safety concerns are about misuse, not about autonomous systems pursuing goals Each camp's beliefs lead to different policy positions, different investment strategies, and different company cultures. This is why the debate is so heated — the stakes are real.

entries.title: 20.6 — What You Can Actually Say With Confidence (2026)
entries.summary: Amidst the disagreement, some things are genuinely known: Current AI is narrow, not general. It excels at specific tasks but cannot generalise the way humans do. It requires specific training, specific context, and specific scaffolding for each new domain. Capabilities are growing fast. Models in 2026 can do things that seemed impossible in 2022. The trajectory is steep. Nobody knows the ceiling.…
entries.sourceText: Amidst the disagreement, some things are genuinely known: Current AI is narrow, not general. It excels at specific tasks but cannot generalise the way humans do. It requires specific training, specific context, and specific scaffolding for each new domain. Capabilities are growing fast. Models in 2026 can do things that seemed impossible in 2022. The trajectory is steep. Nobody knows the ceiling. We don't know whether current architectures will plateau or keep improving. We don't know what's needed for genuine understanding vs sophisticated pattern matching. The alignment problem is real regardless of timelines. Even if AGI is decades away, increasingly capable narrow AI raises alignment and safety questions that matter now. The economic impact is already happening. You don't need AGI for AI to transform industries. Narrow AI is already changing how people work, what jobs exist, and what's possible. 💡 What this chapter ISN'T telling you This chapter is not telling you AGI is coming, or that it isn't. It's not telling you to be afraid or to be excited. It's giving you the vocabulary to follow the conversation — to read the headlines, understand the claims, and evaluate them critically. When someone says "AGI by 2027," you now know: whose definition? Based on what evidence? What would need to be true? That's the value of understanding — not certainty about the future, but the ability to think clearly about uncertainty.

entries.sourceText: AGI (Artificial General Intelligence) AI that matches human intelligence across all domains. Not yet achieved. Timelines contested: some say 2–5 years, others say decades, others say current approaches can't get there. ASI (Artificial Superintelligence) AI that vastly exceeds human intelligence in every domain. Hypothetical. Would represent a fundamentally new situation for humanity. Narrow AI / ANI What exists today. Excellent at specific tasks, cannot generalise. All current AI systems are narrow. Alignment Ensuring powerful AI systems do what humans actually want. Becomes more critical as systems become more capable. Emergence Capabilities that appear unexpectedly as models scale. Abilities no one explicitly trained for. Nobody knows when or if AGI will arrive. The smartest people in the field disagree profoundly. What's known: capabilities are growing fast, current AI is narrow but powerful, and the impacts — economic, social, political — are already real regardless of the AGI question. Check your understanding Question: Someone predicts AGI by a specific year. What is the first clarifying question? Answer: Ask what they mean by AGI and what observable evidence would count. Timelines are meaningless without a definition and test.

entries.title: "Is AI replacing jobs right now?"
entries.summary: Confidence: Solid but moving Not wholesale — and "replacing" is the wrong word for what's happening. It's churn, not subtraction: hiring is contracting in some exposed roles while new work opens up in others, and nobody yet knows which way the balance tips. Most of the panic comes from looking at only one half of that. What's solid — The contraction is real but concentrated.…
entries.sourceText: Confidence: Solid but moving Not wholesale — and "replacing" is the wrong word for what's happening. It's churn, not subtraction: hiring is contracting in some exposed roles while new work opens up in others, and nobody yet knows which way the balance tips. Most of the panic comes from looking at only one half of that. What's solid — The contraction is real but concentrated. Stanford's August 2026 update found a 19% relative employment shortfall for workers aged 22–25 in the most AI-exposed occupations, as of June 2026 — meaning that group's employment ran 19% below where the same group in less-exposed work landed, not that a fifth of them lost jobs. The gap appeared mainly through reduced hiring rather than unusual numbers of people leaving jobs, did not appear comparably among experienced workers, and survived several re-runs of the analysis with the assumptions changed. It is a descriptive study — it establishes that the pattern is there, not that AI caused it. Separately, the World Economic Forum projects 170 million roles created and 92 million displaced by 2030 across five major structural trends — including AI, but not AI alone — for a projected net gain of 78 million. The losses are observed; the global gains remain forecasts. Where it's contested — The losses are already measured while the gains are still projected — so whether creation outpaces contraction, and how fast, is genuinely unknown. There's also real debate about whether the entry-level dip is even an AI effect, or partly a post-2022 over-hiring correction and higher interest rates working through the system. What's unknown — Whether the created roles actually arrive, and whether the people leaving shrinking roles can reach them. The 78 million net gain is a projection built on five structural trends, only one of which is AI. Nobody has measured a completed cycle of this. What it depends on — For you specifically, it comes down to whether AI can do your core task or just speed you up — and whether you move toward the growing side instead of staying put in the shrinking one. The myth to drop — Two of them, actually. "AI is causing mass layoffs" overstates it — this is a hiring slowdown in specific roles, not a wave of firings. But "AI creates more than it destroys, so relax" overstates it the other way — that's a projection, not a result yet. The receipt — Stop asking "will AI take my job" and start asking "where's the new work, and am I moving toward it?" The risk and the opportunity here are the same force, and which one you get depends on where you point yourself. Cher had a closet computer in 1995; being early to the new work has always been the move. Related on LAiDIES: the same tools now let one person do what used to take a whole team — what that opens up . Sources Stanford Digital Economy Lab — August 2026 update WEF — Future of Jobs Report 2025 McKinsey — Generative AI and the future of work in America (2023) Verified August 2026. Recheck when the next Stanford "Canaries" update and the next WEF Future of Jobs land.

entries.title: "Which jobs are most affected?"
entries.summary: Confidence: Solid but moving If your job is mostly "take information from here and put it there," that's where AI reaches first. But the same shift is growing whole categories of other work — so it's a reshuffle, not just a cull. What's solid — According to the WEF, the fastest-shrinking roles are clerical: data entry, admin and secretarial work, cashiers, bank tellers.…
entries.sourceText: Confidence: Solid but moving If your job is mostly "take information from here and put it there," that's where AI reaches first. But the same shift is growing whole categories of other work — so it's a reshuffle, not just a cull. What's solid — According to the WEF, the fastest-shrinking roles are clerical: data entry, admin and secretarial work, cashiers, bank tellers. The fastest-growing, proportionally, are AI and machine-learning specialists and data analysts — but it isn't only tech. Care work, teaching, the skilled trades, and green-energy jobs are all expanding at the same time. Where it's contested — The open question is how fast the growing roles can absorb the people leaving the shrinking ones — retraining doesn't happen overnight, and the two don't always sit in the same place or pay the same. What's unknown — How fast the growing roles can absorb people from the shrinking ones. Retraining timelines, geography and pay bands are all unmeasured here — the WEF projects the shape of the shift, not whether individual people successfully make it. What it depends on — How routine your core tasks are. The more your day is "move information from A to B," the more exposed you are; work that leans on judgment, relationships or physical activity is generally less exposed to current generative AI. Less exposed is not the same as safe or guaranteed to grow. The myth to drop — That this is a blue-collar story, or a white-collar one. It cuts across both — sorted by the kind of task, not the colour of the collar. The receipt — Audit your own week. The "move info from A to B" parts are the exposed parts — and the signal to shift your time toward the judgment and relationship work that's actually growing. Related on LAiDIES: the Wednesday Bag has you practise exactly that shift. Sources WEF — Future of Jobs Report 2025 Verified June 2026. Recheck when the next WEF Future of Jobs report lands.

entries.title: "Will AI replace ME specifically?"
entries.summary: Confidence: Mixed evidence Probably not — and if you're genuinely good at what you do, AI is more likely to extend your reach than erase your job. What it changes is the shape of the work: it takes the rough draft and the grunt-work, you bring the judgment. But how much it helps you depends a lot on whether your work is routine or expert. entries.sourceText: Confidence: Mixed evidence Probably not — and if you're genuinely good at what you do, AI is more likely to extend your reach than erase your job. What it changes is the shape of the work: it takes the rough draft and the grunt-work, you bring the judgment. But how much it helps you depends a lot on whether your work is routine or expert. What's solid — The effect depends on the task. In customer support, AI raised productivity most for newer and lower-skilled workers — about 34% in one study — while experienced workers gained little. A newer study of public-software developers found larger measurable gains among developers with more GitHub experience, while Harvard research found that AI can help adjacent outsiders attempt unfamiliar work without turning distant novices into experts. Across 83 medical studies, large language models performed similarly to non-expert physicians on average but remained roughly 15 points behind specialists, with wide variation between studies and serious quality caveats — three-quarters of those 83 studies were rated at high risk of bias. Where it's contested — Which way it cuts. Whether AI lifts the least experienced or compounds the advantage of the most experienced is genuinely unsettled: the customer-support finding and the developer finding point in opposite directions, and both are good studies. The honest conclusion is that AI can raise the floor or raise the ceiling depending on the task, the tool and the worker — and that no one can yet tell you which yours is. What's unknown — How it nets out by field over time is genuinely unsettled — and whether the value AI unlocks stays with experts or gets competed away as access spreads. A diagnostician's job and a data-entry job are heading in very different directions. What it depends on — Whether your work is mostly codifiable (AI levels it, and the floor rises under you) or mostly expert judgment (AI amplifies it, and your ceiling rises) — and how well you direct and check it, which is exactly where real expertise pays off. The myth to drop — "AI is the great equalizer — now juniors can do what seniors do." The newer evidence says it lets people attempt more, but it can't replace deep expertise; if anything, it rewards it. And stay suspicious of any clean "AI does your job X% as well as you" stat with no real study behind it. The receipt — Deep expertise gives you more ability to brief, test and judge the system — but do not assume that guarantees a gain. Measure the real task. Don't try to out-type the machine; be the expert who can tell when it helped and when it did not. Working with AI 101 teaches that practical loop. Sources Daniotti et al. / Vasilescu — "AI raises the productivity bar," Science (2026) Bojinov & McFowland — "The GenAI Wall Effect," Harvard Business School (2025) Brynjolfsson, Li & Raymond — "Generative AI at Work" (NBER w31161, 2023) Medical meta-analysis — large language models versus physicians Nobel Prize in Chemistry 2024 — AlphaFold (Hassabis, Jumper, Baker) International AI Safety Report (2026) Verified June 2026. Recheck when the expert-vs-novice studies mature.

entries.sourceText: Confidence: Varies by case There is no single honest number per question. National shares can look small while the local burden is serious in a water-stressed watershed. What's solid — Working from Lawrence Berkeley and USGS data, ITIF put US data centres at 17.4 billion gallons of direct water consumption in 2023, plus about 211 billion gallons consumed indirectly generating their electricity — together under 1% of total US water consumption. Note the word consumption : water withdrawn and returned is a different number entirely, and mixing the two is how most viral comparisons go wrong. This is also a US figure, not a world one, and comparisons with agriculture or golf courses need the same geography and the same denominator to mean anything at all. Where it's contested — The famous "500ml per conversation" figure covered roughly 10 to 50 medium-length GPT-3 responses, not one message, and included water used to generate electricity. The authors found large variation by model, location and time. Google measured a median Gemini text prompt in May 2025 at 0.26ml and reported large year-over-year efficiency gains for that service, but that cannot be generalized to every model or workload. What's unknown — Real per-facility numbers are largely missing — disclosure is thin and mostly self-reported. What it depends on — Where the data centre sits (Nordic hydro versus Arizona desert), how it's cooled (closed-loop barely sips; evaporative drinks), and what you count — cooling only, or the electricity's water too. The myth to drop — "Every email you send AI drinks a bottle of water." That's a stretched 2023 estimate for an old model, quoted per message when it was really per dozens. The receipt — Measure AI's water by provider, facility and watershed, not by a viral bottle-per-prompt claim or a national average. Small nationally can still mean heavy locally. entries.sourceText: Confidence: Largely unknown There is no universal number per question. The result changes with model size, response length, hardware, data-centre overhead and the electricity grid. What's solid — Google measured a median Gemini text prompt in May 2025 at 0.24Wh and 0.03g CO₂e — under Google's own choices about what to count, which have been contested; that is a useful product-specific measurement, not an industry constant. For historical scale, researchers estimated that one 2020 GPT-3 training run emitted about 552 tonnes of CO₂e including data-centre overhead. The IEA estimates all data centres produced about 180Mt of indirect CO₂ emissions in 2024 and projects about 320Mt in 2030 in its base case. Where it's contested — No major provider publishes complete, verifiable per-query emissions, so every number out there is a reverse-engineered estimate built on different assumptions. What's unknown — Almost all of it, at the level people actually want. No major provider publishes complete, verifiable per-query emissions, so every number in circulation is reverse-engineered from different assumptions. We have good figures for total data-centre electricity and one company's measurement of one product. We do not have an industry footprint. What it depends on — The grid the data centre runs on. The same question on hydro versus coal is a completely different footprint — David Rose would tell you the specifics are the whole answer here. The myth to drop — Two opposite ones. One product's prompt measurement is not a universal footprint, and "it's just software, so it's clean" ignores the physical system. The IEA estimates widespread use of existing AI applications could help avoid roughly 1.4Gt in 2035, but says current momentum does not guarantee that outcome and rebound effects could reduce it. The receipt — Per-prompt guilt is a rounding error. What actually matters is what powers the data centre and whether clean energy keeps up with the buildout — and, on the other side, whether we point AI at the climate problems it can genuinely help solve. entries.title: "Is AI's energy use getting better or worse?"
entries.summary: Confidence: Solid Both at once — and that's a race, not a verdict. Every query keeps getting more efficient, while total energy use keeps climbing because we keep using so much more of it. What's solid — Efficiency per task is improving, but total demand is growing faster.…
entries.sourceText: Confidence: Solid Both at once — and that's a race, not a verdict. Every query keeps getting more efficient, while total energy use keeps climbing because we keep using so much more of it. What's solid — Efficiency per task is improving, but total demand is growing faster. The IEA put data centre electricity at about 415TWh in 2024 and about 485TWh in 2025 — a 17% rise in one year, against 3% growth in global electricity demand overall — and projects roughly 945TWh by 2030 in its base case. That is a move from about 1.5% of world electricity to just under 3%. Where it's contested — The real unknown is whether clean-energy buildout keeps pace, or whether the surge leans on natural gas and, in some places, revived coal. What's unknown — Where it lands. The IEA's own projection has a wide band, and it depends on choices — grid buildout, siting rules, how much agent workloads take off — that haven't been made yet. Efficiency gains have been unprecedented and total demand has still risen; nobody can tell you which curve wins. What it depends on — Cheaper computation can encourage more use, but rebound is one contributor, not a complete explanation. The myth to drop — "Efficiency gains mean the problem is solving itself." Per-task efficiency and total demand are different measures; one can improve while the other rises. The receipt — Your individual efficiency isn't the lever. The real question is total demand and what powers it — grid, siting, clean energy. That's a policy fight, not a guilt trip. Sources IEA — Energy demand from AI IEA — April 2026 data-centre electricity update UN University INWEH — Environmental cost of AI's energy use: carbon, water and land footprints (2026) Epoch AI — efficiency trends Verified June 2026. entries.title: "Are data centres raising my electricity bill?"
entries.summary: Confidence: Contested The viral numbers often confuse wholesale-market metrics with a household bill. But "data centres do not affect my bill" is too calm. entries.sourceText: Confidence: Contested The viral numbers often confuse wholesale-market metrics with a household bill. But "data centres do not affect my bill" is too calm. The truth is regional, real and still being fought over. What's solid — PJM's independent market monitor estimated that data-centre demand alone increased the cost of the 2025/26 capacity auction — the yearly market where the grid pays generators to guarantee they can meet peak demand — by $9.332 billion, or 174.3%. That was not a 174% increase in consumer prices. Residential prices have also risen in several high-load states, but data centres are not the only cause. Where it's contested — Whether that pressure actually lands on ordinary residents is genuinely disputed. Funding is relevant context: E3's December 2025 report was funded by Amazon, Charles River Associates' February 2026 report was commissioned by the Edison Electric Institute, and E3's May 2026 whitepaper was funded by the Data Center Coalition. Those disclosures do not make the findings false, but they are reasons to read the methods and assumptions closely. EPRI's June 2026 causal analysis reports that rates fell slightly in the locations it studied; that result should be weighed alongside the PJM market monitor's estimate and Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory's work rather than treated as a universal answer. The evidence does not yet support one nationwide conclusion. What's unknown — How much of the wholesale increase actually reaches a residential bill, and over what timeframe. Wholesale capacity costs are 30–50% of a residential bill and pass through slowly and unevenly by utility. The EIA forecasts residential prices rising ~5% in 2026 but does not attribute that to data centres. What it depends on — Rate design, generation and transmission costs, and whether regulators create separate large-load classes or protections against cost shifting. The myth to drop — "If you live near a data centre, your bill jumped 267%." A market metric does not translate one-for-one into a household bill. The receipt — The scary number is wrong; the calm "nothing to see here" is also wrong — and watch who's funding that one. If a data centre is coming to your grid, the real question is "who's on the hook for the upgrades," and that's something you can ask loudly at a utility hearing — Elle Woods walking in with the rate filing tabbed and highlighted. Sources PolitiFact — Warren "267%" fact-check (June 12 2026) E3 — Tailored for Scale (funded by Amazon, Dec 2025) Charles River Associates — Retail Rate Trends in the US (commissioned by EEI, Feb 2026) E3 — Drivers of Rising Electricity Rates (funded by the Data Center Coalition, May 2026) EPRI — Have Data Centers Raised Your Electric Bill? (June 2026) PJM Independent Market Monitor — 2025/26 auction analysis EIA — May 2026 electricity report EIA — Virginia load analysis FERC — large-load proceeding Verified June 2026. Recheck after the next PJM capacity auction and the FERC co-location ruling.

entries.summary: Confidence: Varies by case Not just extraction. entries.sourceText: Confidence: Varies by case Not just extraction. A data centre can bring a community real money — sometimes life-changing money — but the size of the win depends almost entirely on the deal that gets struck, and a lot of it is temporary. What's solid — The Richland Parish windfall is real: construction-linked tax revenue from Meta's project helped raise certified-teacher bonuses from about $10,200 to $50,935 and classified-staff bonuses from about $3,323 to $17,472. Where it's contested — Construction revenue is not the same as permanent recurring revenue. The project has also changed materially since this answer was first written: Louisiana Economic Development said in July 2026 that planned investment now exceeds $50 billion, with commitments for 1,000 operational jobs, 7,500 construction jobs, 5GW of power, over $1.6 billion already contracted with Louisiana businesses and $215 million toward Entergy bill-assistance and efficiency programmes. Meta separately says it is putting more than $1 billion into local roads, water and wastewater — though that figure is Meta's rather than the state's, LED's own project page still gives it as "more than $300 million," and Meta's two announcements on the same day describe the money once as already spent and once as a forward commitment. The long-run result will depend on the final tax, infrastructure and community-benefit agreements. What's unknown — What happens if a big customer walks after the grid investment is committed. Utilities and regulators are visibly building ratepayer protections — Exelon's security agreements cut its data-centre pipeline by 40% — precisely because nobody knows. There is no precedent at this scale. What it depends on — The negotiated deal — community benefit agreements, the size of the abatement, the job and infrastructure commitments, and whether there are clawbacks if the company misses its targets. The myth to drop — Both halves of the argument. "Data centres take everything and give nothing" — Richland's teachers are the receipt against that. And "a data centre is a jackpot for any town" — strip out the abatement and the one-time construction bump and the math thins fast. The receipt — A data centre isn't automatically good or bad for a town — it's a negotiation. The communities that win treat a $50-billion neighbour like the high-stakes counterparty it is: real benefit agreements, real commitments and clawbacks in writing. Miranda Priestly wouldn't accept the first offer, and neither should your town council. The leverage is realest before the deal is signed. Sources KSLA — Richland Parish teacher bonuses Louisiana Economic Development — Meta project page Meta — Deepening our investment in Richland Parish Louisiana Economic Development — July 2026 Meta expansion Verified June 2026. Recheck when Hyperion finishes construction and post-construction tax figures land.

entries.sourceText: Confidence: Solid but moving Maybe — and paying for a consumer plan does not by itself answer the question. Consumer and business products use different rules, and the exact product and setting matter. What's solid — Anthropic says consumer users choose whether new or resumed chats may be used for model improvement, while its commercial products are excluded by default. Retention rules vary by setting and purpose, so the current policy—not a remembered number—is the evidence. Google says saved activity from personal Gemini use may be reviewed by humans and used to improve its services; qualifying Workspace editions are not used to train generative AI outside the customer's domain without permission. OpenAI says API inputs and outputs are not used to train its models by default. For ChatGPT personal plans, check the current Data Controls in the exact account rather than inferring the answer from price. Where it's contested — Opting out is not a force field. Feedback, safety review, retention and deletion exceptions vary by provider, product and setting, so the current policy is the evidence—not a remembered default. What's unknown — What is already in the models. Training is not reversible, disclosure of historic training data is thin, and no provider publishes a per-user account of what was ingested before their current terms. Going forward is controllable; going backward is not auditable. What it depends on — Which tool, which tier, whether you've actually flipped the setting, and whether you used a temporary chat. The myth to drop — "I pay for Pro, so my stuff is private." Paying for a consumer plan buys features, not one universal privacy contract. The receipt — Keep genuinely confidential things — client data, your salary, the closed-door conversation — out of consumer chatbots, even paid ones. Check the current controls in the exact product you use, and use an approved business product or a safer workflow when the information is sensitive. OpenAI — API data policy Google — Gemini Apps & your data Google — Workspace generative AI protections Verified August 2026. entries.summary: Confidence: Varies by case It makes things up — but less, and less randomly, than the panic suggests. What's solid — There is no honest single hallucination rate.…
entries.sourceText: Confidence: Varies by case It makes things up — but less, and less randomly, than the panic suggests. How often depends entirely on what you ask: hand it a document to summarize and the top models are very reliable; ask it to recall a fact from memory and it's much shakier. What's solid — There is no honest single hallucination rate. In Vectara's narrow short-document summarization benchmark, current leaders score roughly 2 to 3%, while broader grounded and knowledge-boundary evaluations produce much higher error rates. Search and supplied sources generally improve performance on retrieval tasks, but neither guarantees correctness. Where it's contested — Benchmarks measure different jobs under different conditions. A low rate on short-document summarization is not the chance that your next answer will be wrong. What's unknown — A single honest rate. There isn't one, and there probably can't be — it depends on the task, the model, whether the system retrieved anything, and how you asked. Published rates vary by more than an order of magnitude and mostly measure different things. What it depends on — The task, model, source quality, retrieval method and how the result is checked. A supplied source makes an answer easier to verify; it does not automatically make it reliable. The myth to drop — Two of them. "Newer models basically fixed this" — they didn't. And "AI is basically always making things up" — also wrong; it's situational, and very low for grounded work. The receipt — Treat it like a brilliant, fast, slightly-too-confident intern — fantastic first draft, never the final word. It's Regina George energy: sounds completely sure, occasionally just inventing things. The fix isn't fear, it's habit: web search on, ask for sources, click them, and verify anything that actually matters. (This is the whole subject of Episode 3, "The Burn Book Problem," if you want the full story.) Sources Vectara — Hallucination Leaderboard Vectara — FaithJudge Artificial Analysis — Omniscience Artificial Analysis — Search Index Stanford RegLab — legal-AI hallucination study ECRI — 2026 Top 10 Health Technology Hazards Verified June 2026. Recheck on each major model generation.

entries.sourceText: Confidence: Varies by case Sometimes what looks like a mistake is the AI finding something true that we simply hadn't thought of. The catch is that you can't tell genius from garbage by how it feels — only by checking. What's solid — It has genuinely happened in domains with hard checks. Professional commentators initially thought AlphaGo's Move 37 was a mistake; it proved pivotal and influenced later Go strategy. AlphaTensor found novel matrix-multiplication algorithms that could be formally checked, while AlphaFold's protein-structure prediction work was independently recognized by the 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. These examples matter because their outputs could be tested. Where it's contested — This kind of magic mostly happens where there's a hard answer key — a Go board, a math proof, a protein fold — where truth can be checked automatically. Your email draft has no such key. And the very same trait that produced Move 37, going where no human would, is exactly what produces a convincing fake citation. What's unknown — In the moment, which one you're looking at. That is the whole difficulty. It resolves only by checking against a source, and there is no reliable tell in the output itself — confidence, fluency and detail are all present in both cases. What it depends on — Whether there's a way to check the answer. In a domain with a clear right answer, a surprising AI move might be brilliant; in an open-ended one, surprising is usually just wrong. The myth to drop — Both directions. "If the AI did something weird, it must be a mistake" — not always; sometimes it's ahead of you. And "maybe my chatbot's weird answer is secretly genius" — almost never, if there's no way to verify it. The receipt — Surprising isn't the same as wrong — but you find out which by checking, not by being impressed. This is the real reason to verify everything: not because AI is dumb, but because brilliant and broken look exactly alike until you do the work. (The holy-it's-not-just-search side of this gets its own episode later in the season — "Ask Jeeves Could Never.") Sources Google DeepMind — 10 years of AlphaGo Google DeepMind — AlphaTensor Nobel Prize in Chemistry 2024 — AlphaFold (Hassabis, Jumper, Baker) Verified June 2026. Rarely needs rechecking — these are stable historical examples.

entries.title: "Is AI actually making companies more productive?"
entries.summary: Confidence: Contested Two true things at once: individual people often get real, large gains from AI — and most companies haven't turned that into results. The gap between "this saved me an hour" and "this moved our numbers" is where the money's getting lost, and it's almost never the technology's fault.…
entries.sourceText: Confidence: Contested Two true things at once: individual people often get real, large gains from AI — and most companies haven't turned that into results. The gap between "this saved me an hour" and "this moved our numbers" is where the money's getting lost, and it's almost never the technology's fault. What's solid — Controlled studies show gains on some tasks: customer-support agents resolved 14% more issues per hour on average, while effects varied sharply by worker and task. At company level, adoption is much wider than measured bottom-line impact. McKinsey's 2025 survey found 88% reporting regular AI use in at least one function, but only 39% reported any impact on enterprise-level operating profit (EBIT — earnings before interest and tax, the standard measure of what a business actually makes), and most of those put it below 5%; about 6% met its "AI high performer" threshold. Deloitte's 2026 survey found 37% still using AI at a surface level with little or no workflow change. KPMG's Q2 2026 survey adds a current marker for that gap: only 7% of more than 2,000 business leaders reported established ROI. Organisations reporting clear CEO accountability for AI-informed decisions reported returns more often (14% versus 4%). Both halves of that are the same executives answering the same survey about themselves — an association, not evidence that appointing a CEO owner produces the return — but it reinforces the point that deployment alone is not implementation. Where it's contested — A 2025 randomized trial found experienced open-source developers completed selected tasks 19% more slowly with early-2025 AI tools despite expecting to be faster, but METR's 2026 follow-up says newer tools may be changing the result. Even individual gains need a stopwatch, not a vibe. What's unknown — Whether AI produces aggregate productivity gains at all. The Federal Reserve stated in July 2026 that "there is no established consensus for how AI investment can be identified in aggregate statistics." Firm-level surveys are not the same thing, and the surveys are self-reported. What it depends on — Almost entirely on implementation — whether the workflow got redesigned, whether people were actually trained, and whether anyone defined what success looks like. As the research puts it, AI doesn't fix a team; it amplifies what's already there. The myth to drop — Two opposite ones. "Buy the licences and productivity appears" — that's how you get shelfware. And "AI doesn't actually help anyone" — it can help a trained person, but the gain must be measured. The receipt — The technology mostly works; the rollout mostly doesn't. The difference between the company that wasted millions and the one that didn't is whether its people were taught to actually use the thing — Be the trained super-user, not the unused seat. Related on LAiDIES: that gap between the seat and the skill is what this whole site is for . Sources McKinsey — The state of AI Deloitte — State of AI in the Enterprise KPMG — Global AI Pulse Q2 2026 METR — randomized controlled trial of experienced devs (2025) METR — 2026 experiment-design update Brynjolfsson, Li & Raymond — Generative AI at Work (NBER w31161, 2023) Google DORA Report (2025) Verified August 2026. Recheck when the next big enterprise-ROI surveys (KPMG, DORA, Deloitte, MIT NANDA) and METR update.

entries.title: "Who's actually benefiting financially?"
entries.summary: Confidence: Solid but moving Right now the money is piled in two places: the companies selling the shovels, and the people who actually know how to dig. The "rising tide lifts all boats" version hasn't arrived — but the cost of building your own boat just collapsed.…
entries.sourceText: Confidence: Solid but moving Right now the money is piled in two places: the companies selling the shovels, and the people who actually know how to dig. The "rising tide lifts all boats" version hasn't arrived — but the cost of building your own boat just collapsed. What's solid — Infrastructure suppliers are the clearest measured winners: Nvidia reported $58.3 billion in net income under standard accounting rules on $81.6 billion in revenue in Q1 FY2027. AI software can also scale unusually quickly — Cursor said it crossed $1 billion in annualised revenue — one month's takings multiplied by twelve, which is a snapshot, not an audited year with a team of more than 300 in November 2025, and its press page reported $2 billion by March 2026 — but it is not a 50-person company. Where it's contested — Whether the rest of the economy catches up. McKinsey found 88% of respondents report some regular organizational AI use, while only about 6% met its high-performer definition. Industrial build-out that pays off, or a capex bonfire? Genuinely unsettled. What's unknown — Whether the capital being spent will earn a return. Roughly $730 billion of hyperscaler capex in 2026 is being laid against AI revenue nobody can cleanly measure, and the depreciation schedules the whole argument turns on rest on how long GPUs stay in productive service — for which there is no public data. What it depends on — Where you sit. Selling shovels: winning. Building a focused thing with a tiny team: newly possible. Waiting for the rising tide to lift your salary: still waiting. The myth to drop — "AI is already making everyone richer." The clearest measured gains are still concentrated upstream and among a small set of high-performing adopters. The receipt — You're probably not going to out-earn Nvidia. But the collapsed cost of building is the part that's actually yours: the thing you couldn't afford to build last year — the team, the budget, the tech — might be a weekend now. Related on LAiDIES: the founder story this site was built on. Sources Nvidia — Q1 FY2027 earnings Cursor — Series D Cursor — press McKinsey — The state of AI Verified June 2026. Recheck quarterly for the sector figures and annually for the macro productivity data.

entries.title: "Is AI making us dumber?"
entries.summary: Confidence: Mixed evidence It can — if you let it think for you. Used the other way, it can sharpen you. The early evidence is real, and it's the same story as calculators and GPS, just turned up louder. What's solid — Early studies raise a real caution, not a verdict. A 54-person study on essay writing found the ChatGPT group showed weaker coordination between brain regions on an EEG and remembered less of what they wrote.…
entries.sourceText: Confidence: Mixed evidence It can — if you let it think for you. Used the other way, it can sharpen you. The early evidence is real, and it's the same story as calculators and GPS, just turned up louder. What's solid — Early studies raise a real caution, not a verdict. A 54-person study on essay writing found the ChatGPT group showed weaker coordination between brain regions on an EEG and remembered less of what they wrote. It is a preprint — posted publicly but never peer-reviewed — and only 18 people completed the final crossover session, the one where groups swapped tools and the headline rests. In that session the brain-first group retained stronger recall after gaining AI. A formal critique calculates the study would have needed around 159 participants to support its conclusions. A 666-person study found an association between frequent AI use, cognitive offloading and lower critical-thinking scores, but its design cannot establish causation. In a colonoscopy study, clinicians' unaided detection rate for pre-cancerous growths fell from 28.4% to 22.4% after routine AI exposure. It is observational — the researchers watched what happened rather than assigning doctors to groups — so, as the authors say plainly, something other than the AI could explain it. Where it's contested — The headline study is small (54 people) and still a preprint, so it's a signal, not a verdict. What's unknown — Anything long-term. No study in this literature runs beyond about seven weeks. There is nothing on months or years of use, nothing on primary-age children with general-purpose chatbots, and the first large international dataset — PISA's "Learning in the Digital World" — has not landed yet. What it depends on — Whether you use AI to skip the thinking or to push it further. The myth to drop — Both extremes. "AI rots your brain" is too strong for the evidence we have — and "it's totally fine" is also wrong, because the skill-fade is measurable. The receipt — Use it to extend your thinking, not replace it. Draft with it, argue with it — then do the actual reasoning yourself on the things you want to stay sharp at. Keep some work unmediated; that's the rep that keeps the muscle. It's why the Wednesday Bag asks you to try the move yourself, not just nod along to it. Sources Kosmyna et al. — "Your Brain on ChatGPT" (MIT Media Lab, 2025, arXiv preprint) Gerlich (2025) — "AI Tools in Society," Societies (MDPI) Lee et al. — Microsoft / CMU, "The Impact of Generative AI on Critical Thinking" (CHI 2025) International AI Safety Report (2026) Colonoscopy study Verified June 2026. Recheck when peer-reviewed replications of the MIT study appear.

entries.sourceText: Confidence: Our synthesis, not a finding Four things — and "learn to code" isn't necessarily one of them. The ability to evaluate and direct AI now matters more than the ability to build it. Our take — This is the one answer on the page that is our synthesis rather than a finding. Our practical four are briefing AI clearly, evaluating its output, redesigning a workflow around it, and deepening the domain expertise needed to judge it. That is LAiDIES' synthesis, not a WEF ranking. WEF's 2025 employer survey separately ranks analytical thinking as the top core skill and AI and big-data literacy, cybersecurity and technological literacy among the fastest-growing, alongside creative thinking, resilience and lifelong learning. Where it's contested — Whether "learn to work with AI" is a durable skill or a temporary one. One camp holds that briefing and judging AI output is the new literacy; another holds that as models improve the briefing gets easier and the durable advantage returns to domain expertise. We lean toward the second, which is why deepening what you actually know is on our list. What's unknown — Which of these still matters in three years. Every specific tool skill has a short half-life, and the meta-skills we name below are our reading of the evidence rather than a measured finding. Treat this answer as the most provisional on the page. What it depends on — Your field, but the meta-skill is learning to learn quickly as tools and workflows change. The myth to drop — "You have to learn to code to stay relevant." For most people, directing and checking AI matters more than writing the code yourself. The receipt — Stop trying to memorize every tool. Get good at the four above, and at picking things up fast — that's the skill set designed to survive model releases. It is also the practical syllabus of Working with AI 101 . Sources WEF — Skills Outlook Verified June 2026. Recheck when the next WEF Future of Jobs report lands.

entries.title: 1.1 The Problem
entries.summary: Last month you typed three words into Claude and got back the best email you've ever sent. Three words. Something like "reply to this" after pasting a tricky message from a vendor. entries.sourceText: Last month you typed three words into Claude and got back the best email you've ever sent. Three words. Something like "reply to this" after pasting a tricky message from a vendor. What came back was so perfectly calibrated that you forwarded it without changing a comma. Yesterday you sat down and wrote a detailed brief. Role: senior project manager. Audience: executive team. Tone: authoritative but approachable. Constraints: under 300 words, no jargon, open with the bottom line. You gave it context. You gave it structure. You did the work. And what came back was so flatly generic you deleted it without reading past the second paragraph. Same you. Same tool. Same Tuesday afternoon subscription plan. What happened? If you've been using AI for more than a few weeks, you've felt this. The maddening randomness of it. The sense that you're playing a slot machine where sometimes you hit the jackpot and sometimes you don't, and the correlation between effort and reward seems… loose. You put in nothing and get gold. You put in everything and get beige. You might have concluded that AI is just unreliable. Or that you're doing something wrong but can't figure out what. Or (the most common one) that there's some secret trick you haven't learned yet, some magic phrasing that the people getting consistent results know and you don't. Those conclusions miss something important. The inconsistency you're experiencing is real, but it is not pure chance. There are specific, identifiable reasons why the same tool gives you genius on Monday and garbage on Wednesday, and once you can see those reasons, you can diagnose and often improve the result. That's what this book is about.

entries.title: 1.2 The Advice Everyone Gives (And Why It's Not Enough)
entries.summary: If you've looked for advice on using AI, you've been hit from two directions. From one side: "Be specific about what you want." Give context. Say what good looks like. Tell it who you are and who the audience is. We call this the David Rose move, after the character in Schitt's Creek who is impossibly, pathologically specific about everything. The wine has to be a very specific wine. The sweater has to drape a very specific way.…
entries.sourceText: If you've looked for advice on using AI, you've been hit from two directions. From one side: "Be specific about what you want." Give context. Say what good looks like. Tell it who you are and who the audience is. We call this the David Rose move, after the character in Schitt's Creek who is impossibly, pathologically specific about everything. The wine has to be a very specific wine. The sweater has to drape a very specific way. The brand aesthetic must be "a general store but make it specific." That energy, applied to AI, means telling it exactly what you need: the audience, the tone, the format, the constraints, what "done" looks like. Be David Rose about it. From the other side: "DM me for these 5 prompts that will change your life." The miracle templates. The secret formulas. The LinkedIn guy who promises you're one magic phrase away from replacing your entire team. Copy-paste this, 10x your productivity, you're welcome. Neither is the full picture. The first one (be specific) is genuinely useful sometimes, but you've already discovered it doesn't always work. You can go full David Rose and still get garbage. The second one (magic prompts) is mostly nonsense dressed up as a product. There is no secret syntax. There is no five-prompt solution to a ten-variable problem. The reality is simpler and harder: your message is one input among many. The output depends on the state of an entire system, not just the words you typed. Specificity helps. But it's not the only lever, and it's often not the one that needs pulling. (If you want a deeper dive into the David Rose move and why it helps when it helps, we explored that in Episode 2 of the podcast and in AI Fundamentals 101 in the LIBRAiRY. Neither is required to follow this book.)

entries.title: 1.3 What's Actually Determining the Output
entries.summary: When you press "send," your message enters a system. And the result you get back depends on the state of that entire system, not just the words you typed. There are ten things determining whether you get genius or garbage. Most of them are invisible unless you know to look. Some are about the AI. Some are about you. Some are about the setup between you and the AI that you didn't know you could control. We're going to name all ten now.…
entries.sourceText: When you press "send," your message enters a system. And the result you get back depends on the state of that entire system, not just the words you typed. There are ten things determining whether you get genius or garbage. Most of them are invisible unless you know to look. Some are about the AI. Some are about you. Some are about the setup between you and the AI that you didn't know you could control. We're going to name all ten now. Not teach them (that's what the rest of the book is for) but name them, so you can start seeing the board. 1. What it can see right now. Your message is one piece of what the AI is looking at when it responds. There's also everything else in the conversation so far, any files you've attached, and instructions baked into the platform you didn't write. All of it influences the output. A perfectly clear ask can produce a terrible result if the surrounding context is polluted, contradictory, or overwhelming. 2. What it remembers about you. Some tools remember things across conversations. Your role, your preferences, your past requests. When this is set up well, it means the AI starts from your baseline instead of a generic one. When it's not set up (or it's set up badly), you're starting from scratch every time, or worse, it's remembering something that's no longer true. 3. Which model is doing the work, and in what mode. When you open "ChatGPT" or "Claude," you're not always talking to the same engine. These brands sit on top of multiple models with different strengths. The same underlying model can also behave very differently when a product gives it different instructions, tools and permissions. A chat mode typically answers and waits. An agentic or work mode may plan, act, pause for approval and produce a deliverable across several steps. Choosing the right mode for the task can matter as much as which model you're using. 4. Whether the task fits the tool. AI is excellent at some things (drafting, summarising, brainstorming, reformatting, explaining) and unreliable at others unless it has the right tools and checks (current facts, exact calculations, precise citations, being right rather than merely plausible ). When you get a brilliant result, you may have asked for something it is well equipped to do. When you get garbage despite a great brief, the task may require evidence, tools or judgment the current setup does not have. 5. What tools it has access to. Can your AI search the web? Read your files? Run code? Connect to other apps? The same question produces completely different results depending on whether the AI can actually go look something up or is relying purely on what it already knows. Most people don't know what their AI can and can't reach. 6. Whether it's acting once or working in a loop. A chatbot usually answers and waits. An agent is configured to pursue a goal across multiple steps, often with tools, but it may pause, misunderstand, hit a limit or require approval. Several major platforms now offer both conversational and agentic ways of working. Knowing which one you selected matters. 7. How you specified what you wanted. Not just "were you specific" but how you structured what you gave it. The skill of writing a clear brief for an AI that will work autonomously is different from writing a good question in a chat. It's closer to delegating to a new hire than to typing a Google search. 8. Whether you can judge what came back. AI can sound equally fluent when it is correct, uncertain or wrong. It may hedge or state uncertainty, but you cannot treat tone as a calibrated confidence score. So evaluation—not just “does it sound good?” but “is this right, useful and fit for my purpose?”—is one of the variables. 9. Whether any of this is repeatable. A one-off great result is nice. A system that produces reliably good results across your recurring work is transformative. The difference between "I sometimes get lucky" and "this genuinely makes me better at my job" is whether you've built the infrastructure around these variables or you're adjusting them by accident every time. 10. Whether you're controlling what comes back. AI has a default voice. It's generic, agreeable, hedging, and long. It will validate your bad ideas as enthusiastically as your good ones. It will produce corporate-smooth output that sounds like everyone else's AI output. You can change all of this: control the voice, the format, the length, how it pushes back, and how you iterate without making it worse. Most people accept the defaults. The defaults are the reason so much AI output is beige.

entries.sourceText: Let's go back to your two experiences. The three-word email that worked perfectly. You pasted a long, context-rich message from a vendor. The AI could see the full email chain (context: rich and focused). It was a fresh conversation with no accumulated noise (history: clean). The task was a direct reply, which is something language models are genuinely great at (task fit: strong). The model you were using happened to be a powerful one (model: appropriate). And you immediately recognised the output was good because you have deep expertise in that vendor relationship (evaluation: informed). The variables happened to be aligned. It looked effortless. It wasn't. Everything was just set right. The detailed brief that produced garbage. You asked for a strategy memo, which requires synthesis and original judgment the model doesn't have (task fit: weak). Your conversation had accumulated messages pulling the AI's attention in conflicting directions (context: polluted). The platform's built-in instructions were telling it to be concise, which contradicted the nuanced tone you asked for (invisible instructions: conflicting). The model running your request was optimised for speed, not depth (model: wrong type). The AI had no access to the actual data or documents it would need to write a real strategy (tool access: none). And the output wasn't actually terrible . It was a decent structure that needed your thinking layered on top. But because you expected finished work, you judged it as failure (evaluation: miscalibrated). Variables misaligned. It looked like the tool just didn't work. Same you. Same tool. Not the same situation at all.

entries.sourceText: Each chapter of this book takes one of these variables and makes it visible, understandable, and controllable. Part II is the loop you run on every task: briefing the job, shaping what comes back, and revising it without wrecking what was already good. It is the part that changes what you do tomorrow morning, which is why it comes first. Part III covers why long conversations go wrong, and the one-time setup — persistent instructions, memory, projects — that stops the AI meeting you for the first time every day. Part IV teaches you to choose the right tool for the job: which model, which mode, which effort setting, and which tasks are worth using AI for at all. Part V covers what changes when AI gets tools and autonomy, how to judge whether an output is actually good, and how to delegate with a definition of done. Part VI ties it together: turning isolated wins into a repeatable system, and using AI responsibly at work. By the end, the randomness disappears. Not because the tools become perfect, but because you can see the full board and adjust the right variable when something isn't working.

You've typed something into ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, or Copilot. You've gotten results, some good, some bad. You don't need to be a power user. You just need to have experienced the basic loop of "ask AI something, get a response, decide whether it's useful." If you've done that, you have everything you need to start here.

entries.sourceText: Think of something you recently asked AI to do where you were disappointed by the result. Open a brand new conversation. Not the old one. Don't continue where you left off. Before typing anything, think: what's the minimum this tool needs to do this task well? Not everything you could say. Just the minimum that matters. Give it that context (who you are relative to this task, what you need, what "done" looks like) and ask your question. Compare the result to what you got before. If the new conversation produces noticeably better output, the variable was likely context . The old conversation had accumulated noise that was dragging quality down. You just experienced Variable 1. If the result is still disappointing, the variable is something else. Maybe task fit. Maybe model choice. Maybe the tool doesn't have access to what it needs. You've eliminated one possibility and narrowed the problem. This is diagnostic thinking. It's the skill that makes the difference between "AI is unpredictable" and "I can identify what to adjust." Every time you change one thing and observe what happens, you learn something about how your setup works. By the end of this book, you'll do this instinctively. Add to Your Working With AI Kit Write down the disappointing task, the one variable you changed and what happened. This is your first diagnostic test card —evidence about your setup, not a generic prompt to worship forever. Check your understanding Question: The same request works yesterday and fails today. What should you inspect before rewriting the prompt? Answer: Inspect the model or mode, the active context, available tools, attached material and acceptance conditions. The visible sentence is only one part of the system.

entries.title: 2.1 The Attention Budget
entries.summary: You're planning a trip. You hand your phone to a friend and say "find me a hotel." They're scrolling through 47 open tabs: your banking app, three Reddit threads about sourdough, a half-written text to your ex, a news article from last week, and somewhere in there, a Google Maps search for Barcelona. They could find you a hotel. They might also get distracted by the sourdough.…
entries.sourceText: You're planning a trip. You hand your phone to a friend and say "find me a hotel." They're scrolling through 47 open tabs: your banking app, three Reddit threads about sourdough, a half-written text to your ex, a news article from last week, and somewhere in there, a Google Maps search for Barcelona. They could find you a hotel. They might also get distracted by the sourdough. That's roughly what you're doing when you dump ten documents into an AI conversation and say "help me with this." The AI reads everything you gave it. All of it. And it can't tell which parts you think are important and which are just... still open. This chapter is about what to give the AI for a specific task, and (just as importantly) what to leave out. The instinct most people have is: give it everything. Upload all the documents. Paste the full email chain. Attach every reference. Let the AI sort it out. It has a million-token context window, after all. Here's what's true in August 2026: models have improved dramatically at handling large inputs, and some vendors report very high scores on narrow “needle in a haystack” retrieval tests. That does not prove equally reliable reasoning or semantic retrieval across a million tokens. A full 50-page document can be useful input when the tool supports it, but ask for page or section references and verify important details against the original. But there's a critical difference between giving it a lot of RELEVANT context and giving it a lot of IRRELEVANT context hoping it'll find the relevant bits. That second thing still makes output worse, even on the most capable 2026 models. Controlled long-context evaluations show that more input is not automatically more usable input: performance can decline as irrelevant material grows, even while the content still fits inside the advertised window. The model may not warn you that focus has degraded. It can simply produce a vaguer or less accurate answer, which is why selection matters more than impressive capacity numbers. The practical framing from one 2026 researcher: "Models genuinely have gotten better at self-correction, so a lot of the fussy manual work that once mattered now buys less. But context still shapes results powerfully, and an agent handed a bad context will confidently do the wrong thing no matter how capable it is." Andrej Karpathy (one of the researchers behind the early AI systems that led to today's tools) put it simply: the AI's context window is like working memory. Your job is to load exactly the right information for each task. Not all the information. Not the most information. The right information. That job has gotten easier as models have improved. But it hasn't gone away. This chapter teaches you how to decide what "right" means for different tasks.

entries.title: 2.2 Think Before You Type
entries.summary: A useful separator between improvised and repeatable AI work is what happens before you start typing. The 60-second preparation method below is a practical routine to test, not a measured universal optimum. Most people open a chat, describe what they want, and press send. When the output isn't right, they adjust and try again. The iteration loop becomes the substitute for thinking.…
entries.sourceText: A useful separator between improvised and repeatable AI work is what happens before you start typing. The 60-second preparation method below is a practical routine to test, not a measured universal optimum. Most people open a chat, describe what they want, and press send. When the output isn't right, they adjust and try again. The iteration loop becomes the substitute for thinking. Three rounds of "no, try again" later, the conversation is polluted with failed attempts (Chapter 5's context rot), and the fourth attempt is working against all the accumulated noise. The fix takes one minute. Before you type, answer five questions: 1. What's the actual deliverable? Not "I need help with X" but "I need [a specific thing] for [a specific use]." The difference between "help me with this presentation" and "I need 5 slide titles with one-sentence descriptions for an internal quarterly review, audience is senior leadership, focus is what changed since last quarter" is the difference between generic output and usable output. 2. What does the AI need to know that it can't guess? The audience. The constraints. Why this matters. What happened before. Any context that's specific to your situation rather than general knowledge. If a smart but uninformed colleague would need to ask you a question before starting, the AI needs that information too. The difference is: the colleague would ask. The AI will just guess. 3. What do I have that I could show it? Files, examples, previous versions, reference material, screenshots. Anything the AI could look at directly rather than relying on your description of it. 4. What would distract it? Old versions of documents. Tangentially related files. Context from a different project. Information that LOOKS relevant but isn't for THIS specific task. Everything you include that doesn't directly serve the task dilutes what does. 5. What does "good enough" look like? Are you going to iterate on this? Is it a first draft you'll refine, or does it need to be right the first time? If it's a draft, say so. If there are specific things that would make you reject it (wrong tone, wrong length, wrong audience), say those up front. Sixty seconds. Five questions. The output from this preparation is worth more than any amount of prompt-tweaking after the fact.

entries.sourceText: The word "prompt" implies a single clever sentence that unlocks the AI's potential. The reality in 2026 is closer to writing a brief: a short, structured description that gives a smart but uninformed executor everything they need to produce what you want. An agent can sometimes pause or ask for clarification, but you should not depend on that happening at the right moment. If the brief leaves an important blank, the system may make a plausible choice and continue. Name the ambiguity before it becomes an autonomous decision. A good brief has at most six parts: Outcome. What you want to end up with, described as a result, not a process. "A one-page summary of this report for my CFO" not "read this and tell me what's important." Audience. Who will read/use this output. This changes everything: vocabulary, detail level, what gets emphasised, what gets left out. Constraints. What it must NOT do. Length limits. Things to avoid. Scope boundaries. "Under 300 words. No technical jargon. Don't mention the restructuring." Format. What the output looks like structurally. Bullet points or prose. Sections or one block. Table or narrative. If you don't specify, it'll choose for you (often wrong). What good looks like. If you have an example of the kind of output you want, show it (Section 4.5 covers this in depth). If you don't, describe the quality bar: "The tone of an internal email between peers, not a formal memo to a board." What you've already tried (if relevant). If this isn't your first attempt, tell it what didn't work and why. "I already tried asking for a summary and it was too high-level. I need more operational detail, specifically around timelines and owners." You don't always need all six. A simple task might only need outcome + constraints. A complex task might need all of them. The test: could a smart colleague you've never worked with execute this brief without asking you a single clarifying question? If yes, the AI can too. If not, what question would they ask? Answer it in the brief.
